title: Syllabus
text:
By the end of the course you should be able to:

Explain movement through the movement-ecology paradigm, and name the ecological drivers and trade-offs behind a path.
Choose a tracking design — technology, fix interval, duration — for a species and a question, and state its biases.
Handle spatial data in R — import, reproject, overlay, map — without hand-waving about coordinate reference systems.
Turn fixes into a defensible trajectory: clean it, regularise it, and annotate it with environmental data matched in space and time.
Quantify and classify movement with path descriptors, first-passage time and change-point methods, and test whether the result depends on the sampling.
Simulate movement with random-walk models and use simulations as null models and as ground truth for estimators.
Estimate space use with MCP, KDE, Brownian bridges and AKDE, and say which question each estimate answers.
Fit and interpret resource and step selection functions, including integrated step selection analysis.
Infer behavioural states with hidden Markov models, with covariates on the switching between them.
Work reproducibly: scripted analyses that another person — including future you — can rerun.

title: Syllabus
text:
The spine: the movement-ecology paradigm
Nathan et al. (2008) proposed that every movement path is the joint outcome of four components: the animal’s internal state (why move?), its motion capacity (how?), its navigation capacity (where to?), and the external factors acting on it. Tracking data record only the path. Every session opens by showing which of the four components its methods try to reach.

title: Syllabus
text:
Structure of a session



Minutes
What




0–5
Recap, and where today sits on the paradigm


5–50
Theory, with at least three pop quizzes


50–55
Break


55–120
Practical in R — you type, I circulate



Session 8 ends with mini-project pitches: its practical is shorter (~50 minutes) to leave ~20 minutes for them.

Pop quizzes
Multiple-choice questions are embedded in the slides. Click an option and the deck reveals the correct answer and a short explanation. They are not graded — they exist so that you, and I, find out in real time whether an idea landed.


Practicals
Every session has a practical page with the full R code. Solutions are in collapsible blocks: try first, then unfold. The practicals are cumulative — the track you clean in Session 3 is the one you classify in Session 4 and model in Session 8, and the animal you simulate in Session 5 is the ground truth for Sessions 6 and 7.
The worked examples are starting points. Extending them to another animal, another dataset or another parameter value is exactly what the weekly submissions ask you to do.

title: Syllabus
text:
Assessment








Component
Weight
What




Reproducible report
50%
Your mini-project, as a Quarto (or R Markdown) document


Weekly practical submissions
30%
The “To hand in” item at the end of each practical


Participation
20%
Quizzes, practicals, and your Session 8 pitch




The report

Pick one of the course datasets (or bring your own, with my approval).
Pose one clear question the data can answer, and pitch it in Session 8.
Produce a Quarto document (~4–6 pages rendered) with the question, the cleaning steps, one or two analyses from the course, the figures, and an honest paragraph on the limitations.
Submit the .qmd and the rendered HTML, so the analysis can be rerun.

Within the report: correctness of the analysis (40%), justification of the methodological choices (30%), reproducibility and code clarity (20%), clarity of figures and writing (10%).
Keeping your project in Git is strongly encouraged: a history of commits is the best evidence that your analysis is reproducible, and it is a skill worth having regardless of this course.






Note



The commonest way to lose marks is to run an analysis whose assumptions the data violate — fitting an HMM to wildly irregular data, or estimating a home range for an animal that is not range-resident. Saying “this is a limitation because X” earns marks; silently ignoring it does not. If you can, test your method on simulated data with a known answer first.




Weekly submissions
Each practical ends with a short To hand in item: a figure, a table or a paragraph that extends the worked example. Submit it before the next session. They are marked for completion and understanding, not for polish.

title: Syllabus
text:
Prerequisites
No prior R experience is assumed, but the pace is brisk. If you have never opened R, work through the setup page before Session 1 and budget an evening for the linked introductory tutorial. Basic ecology and statistics (regression, likelihood, the idea of a probability distribution) are assumed.

title: Datasets
text:
1. African buffalo, Kruger National Park
data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz
Six GPS-collared buffalo (Syncerus caffer) in Kruger National Park, South Africa, 2005–2006. Collars reported roughly hourly. This is our workhorse dataset: several individuals, a long series, a confined landscape with strong environmental gradients (rivers, vegetation).






ImportantThe lesson this dataset teaches: duplicates



The raw file contains 3,747 rows that duplicate an existing individual + timestamp combination — about 13% of the file. These come from the tag transmitting the same fix more than once. If you compute step lengths without removing them you get a large number of zero-length steps in zero elapsed time, and your speed distribution acquires an infinite tail.
We fix this properly in Session 3.


Used in: Sessions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8.
Source: Getz WM, Fortmann-Roe S, Cross PC, Lyons AJ, Ryan SJ, Wilmers CC. Movebank study Kruger African Buffalo, GPS tracking, South Africa.

title: Datasets
text:
2. Parti-coloured bat, Switzerland
data/bat_safi.csv.gz
Seventeen bats (Vespertilio murinus) tracked by VHF radio-telemetry near Bern, Switzerland, 2002–2003. Only 1,740 fixes in total.






ImportantThe lesson this dataset teaches: small, irregular, hand-collected data



This is what tracking looked like before GPS, and what it still looks like for any animal too small to carry a satellite tag. Fixes arrive when a human with an antenna managed to get a bearing — so intervals are wildly irregular, nights are dense and days are empty, and individuals have between a handful and a few hundred locations.
Most of the methods in this course assume regular sampling. Applying them here without thinking produces confident nonsense — which is exactly why we use this dataset to practise saying “no, not with these data”.


Used in: Session 3 (as a cautionary counter-example).
Source: Safi K, et al. Movebank study Parti-colored bat Safi Switzerland.

title: Datasets
text:
3. Turkey vulture “Leo”
data/vulture_leo.csv.gz
A single turkey vulture (Cathartes aura) called Leo, tracked by GPS for almost six years (2007–2013) between Canada and Venezuela — over 60° of latitude.






ImportantThe lesson this dataset teaches: one animal, many behaviours



Leo is not doing one thing. He has breeding-ground residency, autumn migration, wintering residency, and spring migration, repeated over six annual cycles. A single home range estimate over the whole track is meaningless — it would describe a “range” covering two continents.
This is the dataset for Session 4: a trajectory that demands segmentation before any other analysis makes sense. It also crosses many UTM zones, which makes it a good test of whether you have understood projections.


Used in: Session 4.
Source: Bildstein K, Barber D, Bechard MJ. Movebank study Turkey Vulture Acopian Center USA GPS.

WarningA real scale-factor trap



MODIS stores NDVI as integers multiplied by 10,000, with −3,000 as the fill value. title: Practical 8 — Hidden Markov models
text:
Goals. Prepare a track for momentuHMM; fit a 2-state model and read it properly; decode and map the states; let time of day drive the switching; compare 2 and 3 states; check pseudo-residuals. Then prepare your mini-project pitch.
Time: ~50 minutes, then ~20 minutes of pitches. Packages: momentuHMM, amt, dplyr, tidyr, lubridate, ggplot2.
library(momentuHMM)
library(amt)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)

title: Practical 8 — Hidden Markov models
Practical 8 — Hidden Markov models
text:
Task 2 — A 2-state model

m2 <- fitHMM(prep, nbStates = 2,
             dist = list(step = "gamma", angle = "vm"),
             Par0 = list(step  = c(20, 400,       # means: state 1, state 2
                                   20, 400,       # sds
                                   0.01, 0.001),  # zero-masses
                         angle = c(0.5, 2)))      # von Mises concentrations
m2
#> Value of the maximum log-likelihood: -76004.51 
#> 
#> 
#> step parameters:
#> ----------------
#>               state 1      state 2
#> mean     16.413393599 3.505018e+02
#> sd       14.055703713 3.253746e+02
#> zeromass  0.004417284 1.484086e-09
#> 
#> angle parameters:
#> -----------------
#>                    state 1   state 2
#> mean          0.000000e+00 0.0000000
#> concentration 3.223576e-17 0.7562868
#> 
#> Regression coeffs for the transition probabilities:
#> ---------------------------------------------------
#>                1 -> 2    2 -> 1
#> (Intercept) -0.186795 -1.914822
#> 
#> Transition probability matrix:
#> ------------------------------
#>           state 1   state 2
#> state 1 0.5465634 0.4534366
#> state 2 0.1284401 0.8715599
#> 
#> Initial distribution:
#> ---------------------
#>  state 1  state 2 
#> 0.229308 0.770692







NoteStarting values



Par0 are initial guesses for the optimiser, grouped by parameter, then by state: both means, then both sds, then both zero-masses. The likelihood of an HMM has several peaks, so bad starting values can land you on the wrong one. For a real analysis, refit from many random starts (retryFits in fitHMM()) and keep the best.


Your turn
2a. Describe the two states. 2b. What is the expected dwell time in each?






NoteSolution






round(m2$mle$step, 2)
#>          state 1 state 2
#> mean       16.41  350.50
#> sd         14.06  325.37
#> zeromass    0.00    0.00
round(m2$mle$angle, 3)
#>               state 1 state 2
#> mean                0   0.000
#> concentration       0   0.756

gam <- m2$mle$gamma
round(gam, 3)
#>         state 1 state 2
#> state 1   0.547   0.453
#> state 2   0.128   0.872
round(1 / (1 - diag(gam)), 1)     # expected consecutive hours in each state
#> state 1 state 2 
#>     2.2     7.8

State 1: steps of a few tens of metres and turning angles close to uniform — the animal barely moves and its direction is noise. An encamped state.
State 2: steps of several hundred metres with some directional persistence — moving.
Expected dwell times: about 2 hours encamped and about 8 hours moving, in units of the sampling interval (here, hours).
The labels are interpretations: “encamped” is consistent with resting, ruminating, or foraging in one spot. Only an independent sensor or direct observation could tell those apart.

title: Practical 8 — Hidden Markov models
text:
Task 3 — Decode and map

prep$state <- factor(viterbi(m2), labels = c("encamped", "moving"))
prep$p_moving <- stateProbs(m2)[, 2]

one <- prep[prep$ID == names(sort(table(prep$ID), decreasing = TRUE))[1], ]
one <- one[1:300, ]

p1 <- ggplot(one, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_path(colour = "grey75") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = state), size = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(encamped = "#1f6f78", moving = "#c1440e")) +
  coord_equal() + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p2 <- ggplot(one, aes(seq_along(p_moving), p_moving)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#c1440e") +
  labs(x = "Hour", y = "P(moving)") + theme_minimal()

patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2, widths = c(1, 1.4))













NoteWhy the probabilities matter





viterbi() gives the single most likely sequence of labels. stateProbs() gives, for every step, the probability of each state. Most steps are near 0 or 1; the ones in between are genuinely ambiguous, and a threshold would have hidden that. Report the probabilities, or at least how many steps are uncertain.

title: Practical 8 — Hidden Markov models
section: Task 4 — Does time of day drive switching?
text:
Task 4 — Does time of day drive switching?
Let the transition probabilities depend on the hour, with a 24-hour cosinor. getPar0() builds starting values for the bigger model from the fitted smaller one.

p0 <- getPar0(m2, formula = ~ cosinor(hour, period = 24))
m2_diel <- fitHMM(prep, nbStates = 2,
                  dist = list(step = "gamma", angle = "vm"),
                  Par0 = p0$Par, beta0 = p0$beta,
                  formula = ~ cosinor(hour, period = 24))

AIC(m2, m2_diel)
#>     Model    AIC
#> 1 m2_diel 151951
#> 2      m2 152031

Your turn
4a. Plot the probability of being in the moving state across the day.






NoteSolution






diel <- stationary(m2_diel, covs = data.frame(hour = 0:23))[[1]]
diel_df <- data.frame(hour = 0:23, p_moving = diel[, 2])
round(diel_df$p_moving[c(1, 6, 12, 16, 19, 24)], 2)   # 00, 05, 11, 15, 18, 23 h
#> [1] 0.76 0.69 0.80 0.86 0.86 0.78

ggplot(diel_df, aes(hour, p_moving)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#c1440e", linewidth = 1) + geom_point(colour = "#c1440e") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 3)) +
  labs(x = "Local hour", y = "Stationary P(moving)",
       title = "Buffalo move most in the afternoon") +
  theme_minimal()







The diel model is strongly preferred by AIC. The buffalo are least likely to be moving before dawn and most likely in the late afternoon and evening. The covariate acts on the switching between states: the steps within each state have not changed, only how much time is spent in each.
This is the bridge between Sessions 3 and 8: any covariate you can attach to a fix — time of day, NDVI, distance to water — can drive the transitions.

title: Practical 8 — Hidden Markov models
text:
Task 5 — Two states or three?

m3 <- fitHMM(prep, nbStates = 3,
             dist = list(step = "gamma", angle = "vm"),
             Par0 = list(step  = c(15, 150, 600, 15, 150, 600, 0.01, 0.001, 0.001),
                         angle = c(0.3, 1, 2)))
AIC(m2, m3)
#>   Model    AIC
#> 1    m3 150809
#> 2    m2 152031
round(m3$mle$step, 1)
#>          state 1 state 2 state 3
#> mean        18.0   191.1   572.2
#> sd          15.8   136.1   399.0
#> zeromass     0.0     0.0     0.0

Your turn
5a. AIC prefers 3 states. Should you report 3? 5b. Check the pseudo-residuals of the 2-state model.






NoteSolution





AIC will usually keep falling as you add states: extra components always fit the shape of the data better. The question is whether the third state is a behaviour:

round(1 / (1 - diag(m3$mle$gamma)), 1)
#> state 1 state 2 state 3 
#>     2.1     2.9     3.4
round(table(viterbi(m3)) / nrow(prep), 3)
#> 
#>     1     2     3 
#> 0.262 0.412 0.326

Here the third state sits between the other two — resting, grazing, travelling is a biologically plausible triplet for a large grazer. If you report three states, say that you chose three for that reason and checked it, not because AIC said so.

pr <- pseudoRes(m2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(pr$stepRes, main = "Step pseudo-residuals", pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
       col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.4)); qqline(pr$stepRes, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
qqnorm(pr$angleRes, main = "Angle pseudo-residuals", pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
       col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.4)); qqline(pr$angleRes, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)






par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

If the model described the data, the points would lie on the line. Systematic departures in the tails say the step-length distribution or the number of states is not capturing the data — useful evidence when deciding between 2 and 3 states, and far more informative than a table of AICs.

title: Practical 8 — Hidden Markov models
text:
Task 6 — Your mini-project pitch






TipPrepare 3–5 minutes, at most three slides





Question — one sentence, answerable with data you can get.

Data — which dataset (course data, Movebank, your own), which animals, what sampling interval.

Method — which session’s tools, and why they fit the question.

Pitfall — what could make your answer wrong, and how you will check it. If you can test your method on simulated data with a known answer first, say so.

Ideas: compare home-range estimates under two fix rates using the simulated animal; an SSF for a second fisher; do the buffalo’s HMM states line up with day and night? do Leo’s migration dates shift across years?

title: Practical 8 — Hidden Markov models
text:
To hand in






TipWeekly submission



Your pitch slides, and the 2-state HMM of Task 2 fitted to one other buffalo, with its dwell times and one sentence on whether the states look like Cilla’s and Toni’s.

title: Practical 8 — Hidden Markov models
text:
Self-check

You want to know whether buffalo are more likely to start moving when NDVI is low. Where does NDVI go in fitHMM()?

In Par0
In formula, so it acts on the transition probabilities
In dist
Nowhere — HMMs cannot include covariates


“More likely to start moving” is a statement about switching, which the transition probabilities govern. formula = ~ ndvi makes them a function of NDVI. Putting NDVI on the step-length parameters instead would ask a different question: whether the animal moves faster given that it is already moving.



Your HMM assigns 97% of steps to state 1 and 3% to state 2, whose mean step is 12 km per hour. What has probably happened?

The animal travels 3% of the time
State 2 is absorbing location errors rather than describing a behaviour
The model needs more states
The sampling interval is too short


A rare state with an extreme mean is the signature of a model mopping up outliers. Clean first, then model — which is why Task 1 drops the 63 km spike.

title: Practical 7 — Habitat selection on the move
text:
Goals. Fit a resource selection function and a step selection function to the same fisher; interpret both with relative selection strength; recover the realised movement kernel; test whether habitat changes how the animal moves; and find out which method recovers a known selection coefficient from a simulated animal.
Time: ~70 minutes. Packages: amt, terra, survival, dplyr, ggplot2.
library(amt)
library(terra)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)

title: Practical 7 — Habitat selection on the move
section: The data: fishers in New York
text:
The data: fishers in New York
amt ships GPS tracks of four fishers (Pekania pennanti) from LaPoint et al. (2013), with three rasters: land use (GlobCover, 300 m), elevation, and human population density.

data(amt_fisher)
amt_fisher |> count(name)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   name        n
#>   <chr>   <int>
#> 1 Leroy     919
#> 2 Lucile   1349
#> 3 Lupe     3004
#> 4 Ricky T  8958

cov <- get_amt_fisher_covars()

# GlobCover classes 40-100 and 160-170 are forest
forest <- cov$landuse %in% c(40:100, 160:170)
covs <- c(forest,
          resample(cov$elevation, forest),
          resample(cov$popden, forest))
names(covs) <- c("forest", "elevation", "popden")
covs
#> class       : SpatRaster
#> size        : 54, 59, 3  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 220, 302  (x, y)
#> extent      : 1775801, 1788781, 2398484, 2414792  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : +proj=aea +lat_0=23 +lon_0=-96 +lat_1=29.5 +lat_2=45.5 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +datum=NAD83 +units=m +no_defs
#> source(s)   : memory
#> names       : forest,  elevation,      popden
#> min values  :  FALSE,  49.067795,   23.639465
#> max values  :   TRUE, 147.865814, 4051.015869

We work with Lupe, sampled every ~2 minutes, resampled to a regular 10-minute interval.

lupe <- amt_fisher |>
  filter(name == "Lupe") |>
  track_resample(rate = minutes(10), tolerance = minutes(2)) |>
  filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3)

nrow(lupe)
#> [1] 774

title: Practical 7 — Habitat selection on the move
text:
Task 1 — A resource selection function
Used locations versus random points within Lupe’s range (third order).

set.seed(1)
rsf_dat <- lupe |>
  random_points(n = nrow(lupe) * 10) |>
  extract_covariates(covs) |>
  mutate(forest = factor(forest, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("other", "forest")),
         elevation_z = as.numeric(scale(elevation)),
         popden_z    = as.numeric(scale(popden)),
         w = ifelse(case_, 1, 5000))

rsf <- glm(case_ ~ forest + elevation_z + popden_z,
           data = rsf_dat, family = binomial(), weights = w)
round(summary(rsf)$coefficients, 3)
#>              Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept)   -12.428      0.577 -21.524    0.000
#> forestforest    1.601      0.579   2.767    0.006
#> elevation_z     0.245      0.035   6.965    0.000
#> popden_z       -0.108      0.037  -2.889    0.004

Your turn
1a. Express each coefficient as relative selection strength with a 95% CI.






NoteSolution






b  <- coef(rsf)[-1]
se <- summary(rsf)$coefficients[-1, 2]
data.frame(term = names(b), RSS = round(exp(b), 2),
           lower = round(exp(b - 1.96 * se), 2), upper = round(exp(b + 1.96 * se), 2))
#>                      term  RSS lower upper
#> forestforest forestforest 4.96  1.60 15.42
#> elevation_z   elevation_z 1.28  1.19  1.37
#> popden_z         popden_z 0.90  0.83  0.97

Relative to what is available within her range, Lupe’s locations are several times more likely to fall in forest than in other cover, more likely at higher elevation (per standard deviation), and less likely where people are dense. The intercept is meaningless — it depends only on how many available points you drew.

title: Practical 7 — Habitat selection on the move
section: Task 2 — The same fisher, as a step selection function
text:
Task 2 — The same fisher, as a step selection function

set.seed(2)
ssf_dat <- lupe |>
  steps_by_burst() |>
  random_steps(n_control = 10) |>
  extract_covariates(covs, where = "both") |>
  mutate(forest_end   = factor(forest_end,   levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("other", "forest")),
         forest_start = factor(forest_start, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("other", "forest")))

ssf_dat |> select(step_id_, case_, sl_, ta_, forest_end, elevation_end) |> head(11)
#> # A tibble: 11 × 6
#>    step_id_ case_   sl_    ta_ forest_end elevation_end
#>  *    <dbl> <lgl> <dbl>  <dbl> <fct>              <dbl>
#>  1        3 TRUE   99.7  0.216 forest             105. 
#>  2        3 FALSE  42.9  2.87  forest             105. 
#>  3        3 FALSE 172.  -2.70  forest              98.9
#>  4        3 FALSE 132.  -1.59  forest              97.9
#>  5        3 FALSE  54.7 -0.242 forest             105. 
#>  6        3 FALSE  19.5 -1.22  forest             105. 
#>  7        3 FALSE 210.  -1.84  forest              97.8
#>  8        3 FALSE  72.2 -0.979 forest             105. 
#>  9        3 FALSE  86.5 -1.59  forest              97.9
#> 10        3 FALSE 353.  -0.341 forest              99.6
#> 11        3 FALSE  11.3 -0.199 forest             105.

One stratum: the step Lupe took (case_ = TRUE) and ten she could have taken from the same point at the same moment.

issf <- fit_issf(ssf_dat,
                 case_ ~ forest_end + elevation_end + popden_end +
                   sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) + strata(step_id_),
                 model = TRUE)
round(summary(issf$model)$coefficients[, c(1, 3, 5)], 4)
#>                     coef se(coef) Pr(>|z|)
#> forest_endforest  1.4803   0.7378   0.0448
#> elevation_end     0.0679   0.0196   0.0005
#> popden_end       -0.0010   0.0008   0.2009
#> sl_              -0.0001   0.0005   0.8262
#> log(sl_)          0.0684   0.0629   0.2771
#> cos(ta_)          0.0361   0.0670   0.5895

Your turn
2a. Compute the RSS for a step ending in forest versus other cover, with a confidence interval, using log_rss().






NoteSolution






x1 <- data.frame(forest_end = factor("forest", levels = c("other", "forest")),
                 elevation_end = mean(ssf_dat$elevation_end, na.rm = TRUE),
                 popden_end    = mean(ssf_dat$popden_end, na.rm = TRUE),
                 sl_ = 100, ta_ = 0)
x2 <- x1
x2$forest_end <- factor("other", levels = c("other", "forest"))

rss <- log_rss(issf, x1, x2, ci = "se")
exp(rss$df[, c("log_rss", "lwr", "upr")])
#>   log_rss      lwr      upr
#> 1 4.39433 1.034846 18.65991

Given two equally reachable destinations, identical in elevation and population density, Lupe is roughly four times as likely to step into forest. The interval is wide: forest covers most of this landscape, so there are few strata where forest and non-forest are both on offer — a reminder that selection can only be estimated where there is choice.

title: Practical 7 — Habitat selection on the move
text:
Task 3 — The realised movement kernel
The control steps were drawn from a tentative gamma and von Mises fitted to the observed steps. The movement terms in the model correct them.

upd_sl <- update_gamma(sl_distr(ssf_dat),
                       beta_sl = coef(issf)[["sl_"]],
                       beta_log_sl = coef(issf)[["log(sl_)"]])
upd_ta <- update_vonmises(ta_distr(ssf_dat), beta_cos_ta = coef(issf)[["cos(ta_)"]])

data.frame(
  quantity  = c("mean step (m)", "von Mises kappa"),
  tentative = round(c(prod(unlist(sl_distr(ssf_dat)$params)), ta_distr(ssf_dat)$params$kappa), 2),
  realised  = round(c(prod(unlist(upd_sl$params)), upd_ta$params$kappa), 2)
)
#>          quantity tentative realised
#> 1   mean step (m)    147.26   154.38
#> 2 von Mises kappa      0.34     0.38







NoteReading it





Here the two kernels are close, and the movement coefficients are not significant: once selection is accounted for, Lupe’s movement is well described by the distributions the controls were drawn from. When they differ, the realised kernel is the one to use for prediction or simulation — it is the animal’s movement with the habitat effect removed.

title: Practical 7 — Habitat selection on the move
section: Task 4 — Does habitat change how she moves?
text:
Task 4 — Does habitat change how she moves?
Interact the movement terms with the habitat at the start of the step. First the obvious candidate, forest:

issf_forest <- fit_issf(ssf_dat,
                        case_ ~ forest_end + elevation_end + popden_end +
                          sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) +
                          sl_:forest_start + cos(ta_):forest_start +
                          strata(step_id_),
                        model = TRUE)
round(summary(issf_forest$model)$coefficients[, c(1, 2, 5)], 3)
#>                                coef    exp(coef) Pr(>|z|)
#> forest_endforest              1.284 3.611000e+00    0.079
#> elevation_end                 0.067 1.070000e+00    0.001
#> popden_end                   -0.001 9.990000e-01    0.209
#> sl_                           0.105 1.111000e+00    0.994
#> log(sl_)                      0.069 1.072000e+00    0.271
#> cos(ta_)                     25.751 1.525347e+11    0.993
#> sl_:forest_startforest       -0.106 9.000000e-01    0.994
#> cos(ta_):forest_startforest -25.721 0.000000e+00    0.993

Your turn
4a. Look at the standard errors of the two interaction terms. What went wrong?






NoteSolution





Standard errors in the tens or thousands mean the model cannot estimate those terms. Count the information:

ssf_dat |> filter(case_) |> count(forest_start)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   forest_start     n
#>   <fct>        <int>
#> 1 other            2
#> 2 forest         519

Almost every observed step starts in forest. With a couple of non-forest starts, there is nothing to compare: the likelihood is flat and the optimiser wanders off towards infinity (quasi-complete separation). The coefficient is not “huge”; it is undefined.
Always check that the covariate you interact with varies among observed steps before you interpret an interaction.



Population density does vary. Standardise it and interact it with both step terms (they define the gamma distribution together):

ssf_dat <- ssf_dat |> mutate(pop_start_z = as.numeric(scale(popden_start)))

issf_pop <- fit_issf(ssf_dat,
                     case_ ~ forest_end + elevation_end + popden_end +
                       sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) +
                       sl_:pop_start_z + log(sl_):pop_start_z +
                       strata(step_id_),
                     model = TRUE)
round(summary(issf_pop$model)$coefficients[, c(1, 3, 5)], 4)
#>                         coef se(coef) Pr(>|z|)
#> forest_endforest      1.4758   0.7385   0.0457
#> elevation_end         0.0677   0.0195   0.0005
#> popden_end           -0.0010   0.0008   0.2014
#> sl_                  -0.0003   0.0006   0.5710
#> log(sl_)              0.0848   0.0647   0.1901
#> cos(ta_)              0.0358   0.0670   0.5935
#> sl_:pop_start_z      -0.0015   0.0007   0.0270
#> log(sl_):pop_start_z  0.1174   0.0757   0.1209

4b. The two interaction terms work together. Translate them into Lupe’s mean step length where population density is low (−1 SD) and high (+1 SD).






NoteSolution






b <- coef(issf_pop)
kernel_at <- function(z) {
  g <- update_gamma(sl_distr(ssf_dat),
                    beta_sl     = b[["sl_"]]      + z * b[["sl_:pop_start_z"]],
                    beta_log_sl = b[["log(sl_)"]] + z * b[["log(sl_):pop_start_z"]])
  data.frame(popden_start_sd = z, mean_step_m = round(g$params$shape * g$params$scale))
}
bind_rows(lapply(c(-1, 0, 1), kernel_at))
#>   popden_start_sd mean_step_m
#> 1              -1         170
#> 2               0         152
#> 3               1         141

Where more people live, Lupe takes shorter steps — she moves more slowly through the populated parts of her range. The effect is modest, and one animal is one animal; but this is exactly the kind of habitat-mediated movement an RSF cannot express and an iSSA can.
Always interpret step-length interactions through the implied distribution, never from one coefficient: sl_ and log(sl_) change the scale and shape together, and only their combination has a meaning.

title: Practical 7 — Habitat selection on the move
text:
Task 5 — Is there enough contrast?
A step selection function can only detect selection for a covariate that varies within one step’s reach. The land-use raster has 300 m cells.

same_cell <- cellFromXY(covs, cbind(ssf_dat$x1_, ssf_dat$y1_)) ==
             cellFromXY(covs, cbind(ssf_dat$x2_, ssf_dat$y2_))
c(median_step_m = median(ssf_dat$sl_[ssf_dat$case_]),
  share_in_start_cell = round(mean(same_cell, na.rm = TRUE), 2))
#>       median_step_m share_in_start_cell 
#>            128.3752              0.4800







ImportantMatch covariate grain to step length



About half the control steps never leave the cell they started in: for those strata the land-use value is identical for the used step and its alternatives, and they carry no information about forest selection. Elevation, on a much finer grid, is estimated far more precisely. When covariates are coarser than your steps, either get finer covariates or ask a coarser question — never “solve” it by quietly making the steps longer.

title: Practical 7 — Habitat selection on the move
section: Task 6 — Ground truth: which method recovers a known coefficient?
text:
Task 6 — Ground truth: which method recovers a known coefficient?
R/simulators.R contains simulate_ssf(): an animal that moves with a fixed kernel and, at each step, chooses among 30 possible next steps with probability proportional to \(\exp(\beta \times \text{habitat})\). That is exactly the process an SSF assumes. We set \(\beta = 1.5\).

source("R/simulators.R")
hab <- simulate_habitat()                         # a smooth, standardised habitat surface
sim <- simulate_ssf(1500, hab, beta = 1.5, start = c(0, 0))
sim$t <- as.POSIXct("2026-01-01", tz = "UTC") + (sim$step - 1) * 600
sim_trk <- make_track(sim, x, y, t)


plot(hab, col = hcl.colors(50, "Greens", rev = TRUE), main = "Simulated habitat and animal")
lines(sim$x, sim$y, col = "firebrick", lwd = 0.8)







Your turn
6a. Fit an SSF and an RSF to the simulated animal. Which recovers \(\beta = 1.5\)? 6b. Repeat with \(\beta = 0\).






NoteSolution






compare_methods <- function(beta) {
  s <- simulate_ssf(1500, hab, beta = beta, start = c(0, 0))
  s$t <- as.POSIXct("2026-01-01", tz = "UTC") + (s$step - 1) * 600
  tr <- make_track(s, x, y, t)
  set.seed(3)
  ssf <- tr |> steps() |> random_steps(n_control = 15) |> extract_covariates(hab, where = "end")
  m_ssf <- fit_issf(ssf, case_ ~ habitat + sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) + strata(step_id_), model = TRUE)
  rsf <- tr |> random_points(n = nrow(tr) * 10) |> extract_covariates(hab) |>
    mutate(w = ifelse(case_, 1, 5000))
  m_rsf <- glm(case_ ~ habitat, data = rsf, family = binomial(), weights = w)
  data.frame(true_beta = beta,
             SSF = round(coef(m_ssf)[["habitat"]], 2),
             SSF_se = round(sqrt(diag(vcov(m_ssf$model)))[["habitat"]], 2),
             RSF = round(coef(m_rsf)[["habitat"]], 2),
             RSF_se = round(summary(m_rsf)$coefficients["habitat", 2], 2))
}
bind_rows(compare_methods(1.5), compare_methods(0))
#>   true_beta   SSF SSF_se   RSF RSF_se
#> 1       1.5  1.42   0.11  1.02   0.03
#> 2       0.0 -0.04   0.09 -0.06   0.03

The SSF recovers the true coefficient (within its standard error) because it is fitted to the same process that generated the data: each step compared with its own reachable alternatives.
The RSF does not, and it is not supposed to. It compares locations with everywhere in the range, as if the animal could teleport; the answer mixes selection with the constraint of having to walk. Note also its standard error: three to four times smaller than the SSF’s, for a less accurate estimate. The RSF treats 1,500 autocorrelated positions as independent, so it is confidently wrong.
That is not an argument against RSFs — for broad-scale questions about where ranges sit they are the right tool. It is an argument for knowing which question each method answers, and simulation with a known truth is how you find out.

title: Practical 7 — Habitat selection on the move
text:
Self-check

Removing strata(step_id_) from an SSF formula:

Only changes the standard errors
Fits a different, wrong model: every step is compared with every control step in the dataset
Speeds up fitting without changing the estimates
Turns the SSF into an RSF with the same meaning


The stratum is the design: each used step is compared only with the alternatives from the same place and time. Without it, a step in the forest at dawn is compared with control steps from the other side of the range days later — the local, time-specific availability that made the SSF worth fitting is gone.



An RSF gives a smaller standard error than an SSF for the same animal. Does that make it more reliable?

Yes — smaller standard errors mean more precise estimates
No — the RSF treats autocorrelated fixes as independent, so its precision is overstated
Yes, if the RSF has more available points
Only if the two coefficients agree


In the ground-truth task the RSF’s standard error was several times smaller and its estimate further from the truth. Precision you did not earn is worse than honest uncertainty: it makes a wrong answer look certain.

Task 1 — Five estimates of one home range
MCP and KDE

mcp95 <- mcp(pts, percent = 95)
area_mcp <- mcp.area(pts, percent = 95, unout = "km2", plotit = FALSE)[[1]]

kd_href <- kernelUD(pts, h = "href", grid = 300, extent = 1)
kd_lscv <- kernelUD(pts, h = "LSCV", grid = 300, extent = 1)

area_href <- kernel.area(kd_href, percent = 95, unout = "km2")[[1]]
area_lscv <- kernel.area(kd_lscv, percent = 95, unout = "km2")[[1]]

c(h_ref_m = kd_href@h$h, h_lscv_m = kd_lscv@h$h,
  lscv_converged = kd_lscv@h$convergence)
#>        h_ref_m       h_lscv_m lscv_converged 
#>      1179.1127       117.9113         0.0000

Brownian bridge
The bridge needs the trajectory, not just the points, and two variance parameters: sig2, the location error (we assume ~30 m for GPS), and sig1, the animal’s mobility, which liker() estimates by maximum likelihood.

ltr <- as.ltraj(xy = as.data.frame(xy), date = cilla$t, id = "Cilla")
lik <- liker(ltr, sig2 = 30, rangesig1 = c(1, 100), plotit = FALSE)
lik$Cilla$sig1
#> [1] 4.765766

bb <- kernelbb(ltr, sig1 = lik$Cilla$sig1, sig2 = 30, grid = 300, extent = 0.3)
area_bb <- kernel.area(bb, percent = 95, unout = "km2")[[1]]

AKDE
ctmm fits a continuous-time movement model first. It wants Movebank-style columns and works in geographic coordinates.

tel <- as.telemetry(
  data.frame(timestamp = cilla$t, location.long = cilla$x, location.lat = cilla$y,
             individual.local.identifier = "Cilla"),
  timeformat = "auto")

guess <- ctmm.guess(tel, interactive = FALSE)   # not variogram.fit(): that opens a GUI
fit   <- ctmm.select(tel, guess)
ak    <- akde(tel, fit)

summary(fit)
#> $name
#> [1] "OUF anisotropic"
#> 
#> $DOF
#>       mean       area  diffusion      speed 
#>   12.31357   18.66457  723.22307 3395.27156 
#> 
#> $CI
#>                                          low        est       high
#> area (square kilometers)          286.134732 477.697785 717.553006
#> τ[position] (days)                  3.843246   6.451817  10.830936
#> τ[velocity] (minutes)              43.741209  46.707078  49.874048
#> speed (kilometers/day)             15.443023  15.707215  15.971346
#> diffusion (square kilometers/day)   7.233106   7.790621   8.368539
akde_ci <- summary(ak, units = FALSE)$CI / 1e6   # m² -> km²
akde_ci
#>                           low      est high
#> area (square meters) 241.2526 402.7677  605







WarningDo not use variogram.fit() in a script



It opens an interactive slider window for choosing starting values by eye — great at the console, fatal in a rendered document. ctmm.guess(..., interactive = FALSE) gives the same starting values automatically.


Your turn
1a. Put all five 95% areas in one table. 1b. Did LSCV converge?






NoteSolution






areas <- data.frame(
  estimator = c("MCP 95%", "KDE h_ref", "KDE LSCV", "Brownian bridge", "AKDE"),
  area_km2  = round(c(area_mcp, area_href, area_lscv, area_bb, akde_ci[2])),
  low_km2   = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, round(akde_ci[1])),
  high_km2  = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, round(akde_ci[3]))
)
areas
#>         estimator area_km2 low_km2 high_km2
#> 1         MCP 95%      274      NA       NA
#> 2       KDE h_ref      290      NA       NA
#> 3        KDE LSCV      106      NA       NA
#> 4 Brownian bridge      110      NA       NA
#> 5            AKDE      403     241      605

A factor of about four between the smallest and largest estimate, for the same animal and the same fixes. LSCV did not converge — kernelUD() warned — and chose a bandwidth of about 100 m, which splits the range into fragments around clusters of consecutive fixes. Only AKDE comes with a confidence interval.



1c. Show yourself the autocorrelation problem: thin the fixes and watch the KDE area.






NoteSolution






thin_tab <- lapply(c(1, 2, 6, 12, 24, 48), function(k) {
  keep <- seq(1, nrow(xy), by = k)
  a <- kernel.area(kernelUD(SpatialPoints(xy[keep, ]), h = "href", grid = 200),
                   percent = 95, unout = "km2")[[1]]
  data.frame(every_nth_fix = k, fixes = length(keep), kde95_km2 = round(a))
}) |> bind_rows()
thin_tab
#>   every_nth_fix fixes kde95_km2
#> 1             1  3528       290
#> 2             2  1764       306
#> 3             6   588       331
#> 4            12   294       357
#> 5            24   147       369
#> 6            48    74       389

If the fixes were independent draws from a fixed UD, the estimate would stabilise as you add data. Instead the densest data give the smallest range: every extra autocorrelated fix adds almost no new information but makes the estimator more confident. That is exactly the bias AKDE corrects.

section: Task 3 — Variograms: is there a home range at all?
text:
Task 3 — Variograms: is there a home range at all?

data(gazelle)
gz <- gazelle[[1]]

vg_cilla <- variogram(tel)
vg_gz    <- variogram(gz)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(vg_cilla, CTMM = fit, fraction = 0.5, main = "Buffalo 'Cilla'")
plot(vg_gz, fraction = 0.5, main = "Mongolian gazelle")






par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Your turn
3a. Which variogram levels off? 3b. Fit a model to the gazelle and compare its range-crossing time with the tracking duration.






NoteSolution





Cilla’s variogram rises and then flattens: beyond a lag of a few days her positions are as far apart as they ever get. That asymptote is range residency, and the fitted model’s curve follows it.
The gazelle’s variogram keeps climbing across much of the plot, with no clear plateau. Ignore the saw-teeth: the gazelle was located only every few days, on an irregular schedule, so at some time lags there are very few pairs of fixes and the estimate jumps. Read the overall trend, not the teeth.

fit_gz <- ctmm.select(gz, ctmm.guess(gz, interactive = FALSE))
summary(fit_gz)$CI[c(1, 2), ]
#>                                   low          est         high
#> area (square kilometers) 5.462251e+04 3.034354e+05 761303.53275
#> τ[position] (months)     8.330046e-01 4.780132e+00     27.43041

c(tracking_days = as.numeric(diff(range(gz$t))) / 86400)
#> tracking_days 
#>      351.2088

The gazelle’s estimated range-crossing time is months long, with a confidence interval whose upper end exceeds the whole study. In the time it was tracked, it crossed its “range” only a handful of times — perhaps not at all — so the area estimate spans an order of magnitude. More fixes per day would not help; only a much longer track could. For a nomadic species, the honest answer may be that a home range is the wrong summary.

title: Practical 6 — Home ranges, four ways
text:
Task 4 — Ground truth
In Session 5 we built a central-place walker. Because we wrote its rule, we can compute its true 95% home range by simulating it for a very long time.

source("R/simulators.R")
true95 <- truth_area(0.95)
true95
#> [1] 805.22

Now pretend it is a collared animal: sample it every hour for ~69 days and estimate its range.

sim <- truth_animal()                           # 5,000 steps of 20 minutes
obs <- sim[seq(1, nrow(sim), by = 3), ]         # an hourly GPS fix
obs$t <- as.POSIXct("2026-01-01", tz = "UTC") + (obs$step - 1) * 20 * 60

sim_pts <- SpatialPoints(obs[, c("x", "y")])
est <- c(
  MCP      = mcp.area(sim_pts, percent = 95, unout = "km2", plotit = FALSE)[[1]],
  KDE_href = kernel.area(kernelUD(sim_pts, h = "href", grid = 200), percent = 95, unout = "km2")[[1]],
  KDE_LSCV = kernel.area(suppressWarnings(kernelUD(sim_pts, h = "LSCV", grid = 200)),
                         percent = 95, unout = "km2")[[1]]
)

# AKDE: park the simulated animal in UTM 36S so ctmm gets longitude/latitude
ll <- st_coordinates(st_transform(
  st_as_sf(data.frame(x = obs$x + 4e5, y = obs$y + 7.3e6), coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32736),
  4326))
sim_tel <- as.telemetry(data.frame(timestamp = obs$t, location.long = ll[, 1],
                                   location.lat = ll[, 2], individual.local.identifier = "truth"),
                        timeformat = "auto")
sim_fit <- ctmm.select(sim_tel, ctmm.guess(sim_tel, interactive = FALSE))
sim_ci  <- summary(akde(sim_tel, sim_fit), units = FALSE)$CI / 1e6

round(c(est, AKDE = sim_ci[2], AKDE_low = sim_ci[1], AKDE_high = sim_ci[3],
        TRUTH = true95))
#>       MCP  KDE_href  KDE_LSCV      AKDE  AKDE_low AKDE_high     TRUTH 
#>       661       800       491      1229       493      2295       805

One animal is one draw: an estimator can be lucky. The fair test repeats the experiment on many independent animals. That takes ~20 minutes, so it has been run for you by R/hr_ground_truth.R; the results are in data/hr_ground_truth.csv.

reps <- read.csv("data/hr_ground_truth.csv")
nrow(reps)
#> [1] 20

Your turn
4a. For each estimator, plot estimate / truth across the replicates. 4b. How often does AKDE’s 95% confidence interval contain the truth?






NoteSolution






long <- reps |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(MCP, KDE_href, KDE_LSCV, BBMM, AKDE),
                      names_to = "estimator", values_to = "km2") |>
  mutate(ratio = km2 / true95,
         estimator = factor(estimator, c("MCP", "KDE_href", "KDE_LSCV", "BBMM", "AKDE")))

ggplot(long, aes(estimator, ratio)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#1f6f78", alpha = 0.25, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.12, size = 1.6, colour = "#1f6f78") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Estimate / true area",
       title = "Twenty simulated animals, 69 days of hourly fixes each") +
  theme_minimal()








long |>
  group_by(estimator) |>
  summarise(median_ratio = round(median(ratio), 2),
            spread_IQR   = round(IQR(ratio), 2), .groups = "drop")
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   estimator median_ratio spread_IQR
#>   <fct>            <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 MCP               0.87       0.31
#> 2 KDE_href          0.98       0.31
#> 3 KDE_LSCV          0.64       0.17
#> 4 BBMM              0.42       0.08
#> 5 AKDE              1.57       0.98

c(AKDE_CI_covers_truth = mean(reps$AKDE_low <= reps$true95 & reps$AKDE_high >= reps$true95))
#> AKDE_CI_covers_truth 
#>                  0.9

Every estimator fails in a characteristic way, and now you can see which way:


MCP and KDE with LSCV sit mostly below the line — LSCV in every single replicate. LSCV’s tiny bandwidth fragments the utilisation distribution around clusters of autocorrelated fixes.

The Brownian bridge sits far below, and tightly: about 40% of the true area, every time. It is not wrong — it answers a different question, where the animal went in 69 days, not where it lives.

KDE with \(h_\text{ref}\) is close to the truth on average. That is not luck: \(h_\text{ref}\) is the optimal bandwidth for a single, roughly circular hump, which is exactly what this central-place walker produces. Real ranges such as Cilla’s are lumpy and multimodal, and there \(h_\text{ref}\) over-smooths. A method that works on the animal it assumes can fail on the animal you have.

AKDE is the surprise. Its point estimates run high and vary a lot from animal to animal — yet its 95% confidence interval contains the truth in about 90% of replicates, close to what it promises.

Why? 69 days is only about seven range-crossing times, so the effective sample size is tiny, and AKDE says so: its intervals are wide because the data are thin. The other estimators are just as uncertain; they simply do not tell you. AKDE’s correction also assumes a continuous-time Gaussian movement model, and our walker is not one — even the most principled estimator rests on a movement model, and misspecifying it costs accuracy.
So the lesson is not “AKDE wins”. It is:


no estimator is right in general — each is right for a question and an assumption;

an honest interval beats a precise-looking number;

simulation with a known truth is how you find out which failure you are exposed to — try it with longer tracks (more range crossings) and see how the picture changes.

title: Practical 6 — Home ranges, four ways
text:
Self-check

You double the fix rate of your collars from hourly to every 30 minutes, for the same 3 months. What happens to AKDE’s confidence interval on the home-range area?

It halves
It narrows by a factor of √2
It barely changes, because the effective sample size depends on how many times the animal crossed its range
It widens


AKDE’s effective sample size is roughly the tracking duration divided by the range-crossing time. Sampling faster adds fixes, but not range crossings. To narrow the interval you must track for longer, not more often.



Which estimator would you use to map the corridors an animal actually used during a 2-week dispersal event?

AKDE
A Brownian bridge
MCP
KDE with LSCV


A dispersal event is non-stationary by definition, so a range distribution is meaningless; you want the occurrence distribution — where the animal went — which is exactly what the Brownian bridge estimates.

title: Practical 5 — Simulating movement
section: Task 1 — A correlated random walk, from scratch
text:
Task 1 — A correlated random walk, from scratch
Three ingredients: step lengths (gamma), turning angles (von Mises), and a running sum. Write it before you look at the solution.

simulate_crw <- function(n, shape = 2, scale = 250, kappa = 2) {
  # 1. draw n - 1 turning angles from a von Mises centred on 0
  # 2. heading = cumulative sum of turns, starting from 0
  # 3. draw n step lengths from a gamma
  # 4. x and y = cumulative sums of step * cos(heading), step * sin(heading)
}







NoteSolution






rvm <- function(n, mu = 0, kappa = 1) {
  a <- as.numeric(rvonmises(n, circular(mu), kappa))   # circular -> plain numbers
  atan2(sin(a), cos(a))                                 # wrap to (-pi, pi]
}

simulate_crw <- function(n, shape = 2, scale = 250, kappa = 2) {
  turn    <- rvm(n - 1, 0, kappa)
  heading <- cumsum(c(0, turn))
  sl      <- rgamma(n, shape = shape, scale = scale)
  data.frame(step = seq_len(n),
             x = cumsum(sl * cos(heading)),
             y = cumsum(sl * sin(heading)),
             sl = sl)
}

set.seed(42)
simulate_crw(5)
#>   step        x           y         sl
#> 1    1 1247.641    0.000000 1247.64067
#> 2    2 1583.853  117.168490  356.04362
#> 3    3 1691.825   74.300009  116.17142
#> 4    4 1701.033    4.597192   70.30837
#> 5    5 2067.733 -801.617407  885.69208

Two traps worth knowing. circular::rvonmises() returns a circular object that misbehaves in ordinary arithmetic — convert it with as.numeric(). And its values lie in \([0, 2\pi)\), so wrap them to \((-\pi, \pi]\) before treating them as turns left and right.
The finished version of this function, and the others in this practical, lives in R/simulators.R. Sessions 6 and 7 source() that file.

Task 2 — Persistence makes straightness

set.seed(1)
kappas <- c(0, 1, 3, 10)

sims <- lapply(kappas, function(k) {
  bind_rows(lapply(1:20, function(i) simulate_crw(200, kappa = k)), .id = "sim") |>
    mutate(kappa = k)
}) |> bind_rows()

ggplot(sims, aes(x / 1000, y / 1000, group = sim)) +
  geom_path(alpha = 0.3, colour = "#1f6f78") +
  facet_wrap(~ paste("κ =", kappa), nrow = 1) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "km", y = "km", title = "Twenty 200-step walks at each κ") +
  theme_minimal()







Your turn
2a. Compute the straightness index (net displacement / path length) for each walk and summarise it by κ.






NoteSolution






sims |>
  group_by(kappa, sim) |>
  summarise(net = sqrt(last(x)^2 + last(y)^2), path = sum(sl), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(kappa) |>
  summarise(median_straightness = round(median(net / path), 3))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   kappa median_straightness
#>   <dbl>               <dbl>
#> 1     0               0.059
#> 2     1               0.138
#> 3     3               0.195
#> 4    10               0.327

Straightness rises steeply with κ. But even at κ = 10 it is well below 1 over 200 steps: small turns accumulate, and a long enough correlated walk always ends up wandering. Straightness is a property of the walk and of the number of steps you measure it over.

title: Practical 5 — Simulating movement
text:
Task 3 — Mean squared displacement

msd <- function(d, lags) {
  sapply(lags, function(L)
    mean((d$x[-(1:L)] - head(d$x, -L))^2 + (d$y[-(1:L)] - head(d$y, -L))^2))
}

lags <- 2^(0:8)
set.seed(2)
msd_tab <- lapply(c(0, 2, 10), function(k) {
  m <- rowMeans(sapply(1:30, function(i) msd(simulate_crw(2000, kappa = k), lags)))
  data.frame(kappa = k, lag = lags, msd = m)
}) |> bind_rows()

Your turn
3a. Plot MSD against lag on log–log axes. 3b. Estimate the slope at short lags (1–4) and at long lags (64–256).






NoteSolution






ggplot(msd_tab, aes(lag, msd, colour = factor(kappa))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Lag (steps)", y = "MSD (m²)", colour = "κ") +
  theme_minimal()








msd_tab |>
  group_by(kappa) |>
  summarise(
    slope_short = coef(lm(log(msd[lag <= 4]) ~ log(lag[lag <= 4])))[2],
    slope_long  = coef(lm(log(msd[lag >= 64]) ~ log(lag[lag >= 64])))[2]
  ) |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("slope"), \(z) round(z, 2)))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   kappa slope_short slope_long
#>   <dbl>       <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1     0        1          1   
#> 2     2        1.55       1.04
#> 3    10        1.75       1.23

The uncorrelated walk (κ = 0) has slope 1 at every lag: diffusive throughout. Persistent walks start ballistic (slope approaching 2: they keep going straight) and relax towards diffusive (slope 1) once they have forgotten their heading. The more persistent the walk, the later the crossover — at κ = 10 it has not quite finished even after 256 steps.
On a real track, the lag at which the slope drops from ~2 to ~1 estimates how long the animal holds its direction. A slope that drops towards 0 means something a random walk cannot do: the animal stops getting further away.

section: Task 4 — Bias: homing and central places
text:
Task 4 — Bias: homing and central places

source("R/simulators.R")   # simulate_bcrw() and friends
args(simulate_bcrw)
#> function (n, goal = c(0, 0), w = 0.3, shape = 2, scale = 250, 
#>     kappa = 2, start = c(5000, 5000), heading0 = 0) 
#> NULL

In simulate_bcrw(), each new heading is centred on a weighted circular mean of the previous heading and the bearing to goal; w is the weight on the goal.
Your turn
4a. Release an animal 10 km from home. How many steps does it take to come within 500 m, for w = 0.05, 0.1, 0.3?






NoteSolution






steps_to_home <- function(w, n = 3000) {
  d <- simulate_bcrw(n, goal = c(0, 0), w = w, kappa = 2, start = c(10000, 0))
  hit <- which(sqrt(d$x^2 + d$y^2) < 500)
  if (length(hit)) hit[1] else NA
}

set.seed(3)
homing <- lapply(c(0.05, 0.1, 0.3), function(w)
  data.frame(w = w, steps = replicate(50, steps_to_home(w)))) |>
  bind_rows()

homing |>
  group_by(w) |>
  summarise(median_steps = median(steps, na.rm = TRUE),
            failed = sum(is.na(steps)))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>       w median_steps failed
#>   <dbl>        <dbl>  <int>
#> 1  0.05        1282.     22
#> 2  0.1          472       1
#> 3  0.3           76       0

With the weakest bias, nearly half the walkers are still lost after 3,000 steps; doubling it gets almost all of them home, and a strong bias does it in a few dozen steps. The weak-bias walkers wander a long way first: over a short stretch you would not see the bias at all.



4b. Keep the goal at the start point and run the walker for a long time. What emerges?






NoteSolution






truth <- truth_animal()     # a central-place BCRW, 5,000 steps, fixed seed
ggplot(truth, aes(x / 1000, y / 1000)) +
  geom_path(colour = "#1f6f78", linewidth = 0.2, alpha = 0.6) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = 0, colour = "firebrick", size = 3, shape = 17) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "km", y = "km", title = "A home range, from one movement rule") +
  theme_minimal()







A home range. Nothing in the rule mentions an area: the animal simply wanders, with a slight pull towards home. The boundary emerges.
This is our ground-truth animal. Because we wrote the rule, we can simulate it for as long as we like and know its true utilisation distribution — so in Session 6 we can check which home-range estimator recovers it.

title: Practical 5 — Simulating movement
section: Task 5 — Is it a Lévy walk?
text:
Task 5 — Is it a Lévy walk?
Fit two models to step lengths above a threshold xmin, by maximum likelihood: a (shifted) exponential and a power law (Pareto). Both have one parameter, so AIC compares them fairly.

compare_tails <- function(x, xmin) {
  x <- x[x >= xmin]
  n <- length(x)
  # power law: f(x) = (a - 1) / xmin * (x / xmin)^-a
  s <- sum(log(x / xmin))
  a <- 1 + n / s
  ll_pow <- n * log(a - 1) - n * log(xmin) - a * s
  # exponential shifted to start at xmin
  lambda <- 1 / (mean(x) - xmin)
  ll_exp <- n * log(lambda) - lambda * sum(x - xmin)
  data.frame(n = n, mu_hat = round(a, 2),
             AIC_exponential = round(2 - 2 * ll_exp),
             AIC_power_law   = round(2 - 2 * ll_pow),
             winner = ifelse(ll_pow > ll_exp, "power law", "exponential"))
}

Your turn
5a. Test it on data where you know the answer: 2,000 exponential steps, and 2,000 power-law steps with μ = 2. 5b. Now 2,000 steps from an animal that switches between two behaviours, each with exponential steps: 75% short (mean 60 m) and 25% long (mean 1,500 m).






NoteSolution






set.seed(4)
bind_rows(
  cbind(data = "exponential",            compare_tails(rexp(2000, 1 / 300) + 50, 50)),
  cbind(data = "power law, mu = 2",      compare_tails(50 * runif(2000)^(-1), 50)),
  cbind(data = "two exponential modes",  compare_tails(c(rexp(1500, 1 / 60),
                                                         rexp(500, 1 / 1500)) + 10, 10))
)
#>                    data    n mu_hat AIC_exponential AIC_power_law      winner
#> 1           exponential 2000   1.61           26924         28220 exponential
#> 2     power law, mu = 2 2000   2.00           36053         23643   power law
#> 3 two exponential modes 2000   1.43           28076         25856   power law

The method gets the first two right. But the mixture of two exponentials — two ordinary random walks, no power law anywhere — is “identified” as a power law, decisively. That is Benhamou’s (2007) point: a heavy-tailed step-length distribution is what you get whenever an animal switches between short-step and long-step behaviours.
A power-law fit describes the shape of the distribution. It cannot tell you the process. To claim a Lévy strategy you must first rule out that the long steps belong to a separate behavioural state — which is what the hidden Markov models of Session 8 are for.

title: Practical 5 — Simulating movement
section: Task 6 — Is a buffalo range-resident? A simulation test
text:
Task 6 — Is a buffalo range-resident? A simulation test
Null hypothesis: the buffalo moves like a correlated random walk with its own step-length and turning-angle distributions, and no memory of place. Statistic: the radius of gyration of its longest continuous burst — the root-mean-square distance of its positions from their centre.

buffalo <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(id = individual.local.identifier, t = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE)

trk <- make_track(buffalo, x, y, t, id = id, crs = 4326) |>
  transform_coords(crs_to = 32736)

radius_of_gyration <- function(x, y) sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2 + (y - mean(y))^2)) / 1000

null_test <- function(animal, n_sim = 300) {
  hourly <- trk |>
    filter(id == animal) |>
    track_resample(rate = lubridate::hours(1), tolerance = lubridate::minutes(10)) |>
    filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3)
  st <- hourly |> steps_by_burst() |> filter(sl_ > 0, sl_ < 10000)
  g  <- fit_distr(st$sl_, "gamma")                          # the animal's own steps
  vm <- fit_distr(st$ta_[!is.na(st$ta_)], "vonmises")       # and its own turns
  longest <- hourly |> filter(burst_ == names(which.max(table(burst_))))
  n <- nrow(longest)
  obs <- radius_of_gyration(longest$x_, longest$y_)
  sim <- replicate(n_sim, {
    d <- simulate_crw(n, shape = g$params$shape, scale = g$params$scale,
                      kappa = vm$params$kappa)
    radius_of_gyration(d$x, d$y)
  })
  data.frame(id = animal, burst_days = round(n / 24), observed_km = round(obs, 1),
             null_median_km = round(median(sim), 1),
             percentile = round(100 * mean(sim < obs)))
}

set.seed(7)
null_test("Cilla")
#>      id burst_days observed_km null_median_km percentile
#> 1 Cilla         77         7.5            8.6         33

Your turn
6a. Is Cilla more confined than a random walk? 6b. Run the test on all six buffalo, and plot the percentile against burst length. What do you learn?






NoteSolution





Cilla’s radius of gyration is smaller than the simulated median, but about a third of the random walks are more compact still (the exact share varies a little from run to run). With 77 days of data we cannot reject the null.

set.seed(7)
all_tests <- bind_rows(lapply(unique(trk$id), null_test))
all_tests
#>       id burst_days observed_km null_median_km percentile
#> 1  Queen         38         7.4            7.2         53
#> 2   Gabs         36         5.4            4.5         73
#> 3  Cilla         77         7.5            9.0         26
#> 4  Mvubu         49         7.3            6.8         58
#> 5   Toni        157         5.6           10.4          1
#> 6 Pepper          8         2.0            3.3          8


ggplot(all_tests, aes(burst_days, percentile, label = id)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(2.5, 50), linetype = c(2, 3), colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#1f6f78") +
  geom_text(nudge_y = 5) +
  labs(x = "Length of continuous burst (days)",
       y = "Percentile within the CRW null",
       title = "Confinement shows only in long tracks") +
  theme_minimal()







Only Toni, with 157 days of continuous data, is clearly more confined than a random walk. The others were tracked for weeks, not months, and over a few weeks a resident and a random walker cover similar ground: the resident has not yet had time to reach the edges of its range.
This is the tracking duration versus occupation timescale problem. It is not a failure of the test; it is the test telling you your data are too short to answer the question. Session 6’s variogram diagnoses the same thing.

title: Practical 5 — Simulating movement
text:
Self-check

You simulate 1,000 CRWs as a null and your animal’s statistic falls at the 40th percentile. What can you conclude?

The animal is a correlated random walker
The data do not let you distinguish the animal from the null for this statistic
The simulation was too small
The animal is range-resident


Failing to reject a null is not evidence that the null is true. The animal might be doing something else entirely that this statistic cannot detect — or the track may simply be too short. Report it as “consistent with”, never as “is”.



Why must the null CRW use the animal’s own fitted step and turn distributions?

To make the simulation faster
So that the null differs from the animal only in the mechanism being tested
Because simulate_crw() requires them
It does not matter which distributions you use


If the null used shorter steps than the animal, the animal would look “less confined” simply because it moves further per hour. A null must match the animal in everything except the mechanism under test — here, memory of place — or rejecting it tells you nothing.

Task 1 — Net squared displacement
adehabitatLT computes NSD for you: it is the R2n column.

cilla <- trk |> filter(id == "Cilla")
ltr <- as.ltraj(xy = as.data.frame(cilla[, c("x_", "y_")]),
                date = cilla$t_, id = "Cilla")
nsd_cilla <- ld(ltr) |> transmute(t = date, nsd_km2 = R2n / 1e6)

leo_ltr <- as.ltraj(xy = as.data.frame(leo[, c("x_", "y_")]),
                    date = leo$t_, id = "Leo")
nsd_leo <- ld(leo_ltr) |> transmute(t = date, nsd_km2 = R2n / 1e6)


bind_rows(mutate(nsd_cilla, who = "Buffalo 'Cilla'"),
          mutate(nsd_leo,   who = "Vulture 'Leo'")) |>
  ggplot(aes(t, nsd_km2)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#1f6f78", linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ who, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "NSD (km²)") +
  theme_minimal()







Your turn
1a. Describe each curve in one sentence. Which looks resident, which migratory?






NoteSolution





Cilla’s NSD rises quickly to a ceiling and fluctuates below it: once she has explored her range she cannot get further from the start — a resident.
Leo’s NSD shows six annual cycles: a rise (autumn migration), a plateau (wintering), a fall (spring migration), a plateau (breeding) — the textbook migratory profile. The next task makes that judgement quantitative.

title: Practical 4 — Quantifying movement
section: Task 2 — Classify the strategy by fitting models
text:
Task 2 — Classify the strategy by fitting models
Bunnefeld et al. (2011): fit one model per strategy and compare. We fit on daily mean positions to keep the curves manageable.

daily_nsd <- function(tr) {
  d <- tr |>
    mutate(day = as_date(t_)) |>
    group_by(day) |>
    summarise(x = mean(x_), y = mean(y_), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(day)
  data.frame(t = as.numeric(d$day - d$day[1]),
             nsd = ((d$x - d$x[1])^2 + (d$y - d$y[1])^2) / 1e6)   # km²
}

fit_strategies <- function(d) {
  D <- max(d$nsd)
  ctl <- nls.control(maxiter = 500, warnOnly = TRUE)
  half_up   <- d$t[which.max(d$nsd > D / 2)]
  half_down <- d$t[nrow(d) - which.max(rev(d$nsd) > D / 2) + 1]
  fits <- list(
    nomad     = try(nls(nsd ~ b * t, d, start = list(b = D / max(d$t))), silent = TRUE),
    resident  = try(nls(nsd ~ c * (1 - exp(-k * t)), d,
                        start = list(c = median(d$nsd), k = 0.05), control = ctl), silent = TRUE),
    disperser = try(nls(nsd ~ dd / (1 + exp((th - t) / ph)), d,
                        start = list(dd = D, th = half_up, ph = 5), control = ctl), silent = TRUE),
    migrant   = try(nls(nsd ~ dd / (1 + exp((th1 - t) / ph1)) - dd / (1 + exp((th2 - t) / ph2)), d,
                        start = list(dd = D, th1 = half_up, ph1 = 5, th2 = half_down, ph2 = 5),
                        control = ctl), silent = TRUE)
  )
  fits[!vapply(fits, inherits, logical(1), "try-error")]
}

aic_table <- function(fits) {
  a <- vapply(fits, AIC, numeric(1))
  data.frame(model = names(a), dAIC = round(a - min(a))) |> arrange(dAIC)
}

Leo, June 2007 to June 2008:

leo_07 <- leo |> filter(t_ >= as.POSIXct("2007-06-01", tz = "UTC"),
                        t_ <  as.POSIXct("2008-06-01", tz = "UTC"))
fits_leo <- suppressWarnings(fit_strategies(daily_nsd(leo_07)))
aic_table(fits_leo)
#>               model dAIC
#> migrant     migrant    0
#> disperser disperser 2183
#> resident   resident 2326
#> nomad         nomad 2402

The migrant model wins by a mile. Now read its parameters:

cf <- coef(fits_leo$migrant)
c(migration_distance_km = sqrt(cf[["dd"]]),
  departs_day = cf[["th1"]], returns_day = cf[["th2"]])
#> migration_distance_km           departs_day           returns_day 
#>             6145.4027              129.4811              292.6636

as.Date("2007-06-01") + round(c(cf[["th1"]], cf[["th2"]]))   # as calendar dates
#> [1] "2007-10-08" "2008-03-20"

Your turn
2a. Fit the four models to every buffalo. What wins? 2b. For the “migrants”, what is the migration distance? Are they migrants? 2c. Fit Leo’s 2011–2012 year. What goes wrong, and why?






NoteSolution






strategy_summary <- function(tr, label) {
  f <- suppressWarnings(fit_strategies(daily_nsd(tr)))
  a <- aic_table(f)
  best <- a$model[1]
  dist <- if (best == "migrant" || best == "disperser") sqrt(abs(coef(f[[best]])[["dd"]])) else NA
  data.frame(animal = label, days = nrow(daily_nsd(tr)), best = best,
             runner_up_dAIC = a$dAIC[2], displacement_km = round(dist, 1))
}

bind_rows(lapply(unique(trk$id), \(i) strategy_summary(filter(trk, id == i), i)))
#>   animal days      best runner_up_dAIC displacement_km
#> 1  Queen  215   migrant              3            11.8
#> 2   Gabs  158   migrant             27            10.4
#> 3  Cilla  147 disperser              1            10.5
#> 4  Mvubu  107     nomad              4              NA
#> 5   Toni  244   migrant             97            14.0
#> 6 Pepper  361  resident             60              NA

Three buffalo come out as migrants — with “migration” distances of 10 to 14 km. That is a shift to another part of the home range for a few weeks or months, not a migration. The double-sigmoid is the most flexible of the four curves, so it fits any excursion-and-return, and with hundreds of autocorrelated daily points AIC differences are hugely inflated.
Look also at runner_up_dAIC: for several buffalo the second-best model is within a few AIC units of the winner. The data barely separate the stories.

leo_11 <- leo |> filter(t_ >= as.POSIXct("2011-06-01", tz = "UTC"),
                        t_ <  as.POSIXct("2012-06-01", tz = "UTC"))
strategy_summary(leo_11, "Leo 2011-12")
#>        animal days      best runner_up_dAIC displacement_km
#> 1 Leo 2011-12  136 disperser            179          3721.2
range(leo_11$t_)
#> [1] "2011-06-01 00:00:00 UTC" "2011-10-18 11:00:00 UTC"

Leo, a known migrant, is classified as a disperser in 2011–12. The reason is in the dates: that year’s data stop in the middle of the season, so only the outbound half of the cycle is present — which is a single sigmoid step. An incomplete cycle cannot show a return.
The lesson: model-based NSD classification is powerful, but only on complete cycles, and only if you read the parameters. A classification without a displacement distance and dates is not a result.

     main = "Leo: daily displacement", xlab = "log10(km + 1)")
hist(log10(cilla_hourly_speed$km_h + 0.001), breaks = 50, col = "#1f6f78",
     border = "white", main = "Cilla: hourly speed", xlab = "log10(km/h)")






par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Your turn
5a. Where would you put a threshold for each animal? Can you defend it?






NoteSolution





Leo’s histogram has two clearly separated modes — resident days of a few kilometres, migration days of a hundred or more — with an empty valley in between. Any threshold in the valley gives the same answer, so a threshold is transparent and honest:

leo_daily |>
  filter(km > 50) |>
  count(month = month(day, label = TRUE), name = "migration_days")
#> # A tibble: 9 × 2
#>   month migration_days
#>   <ord>          <int>
#> 1 Jan                6
#> 2 Feb                6
#> 3 Mar               47
#> 4 Apr               84
#> 5 May                5
#> 6 Sep               12
#> 7 Oct              109
#> 8 Nov               66
#> 9 Dec               12

Migration days fall in spring and autumn, exactly as the NSD model said.
Cilla’s hourly speeds form one broad, skewed hump. There is no valley, so wherever you put the line, you have made the answer rather than found it. That is precisely the situation in which you need a model that assigns states probabilistically and uses the fact that behaviour persists in time — Session 8’s hidden Markov models.

title: Practical 4 — Quantifying movement
text:
Task 6 — Behavioural change-point analysis
BCPA on persistence velocity \(V\cos\theta\), for the first 25 days of Cilla’s hourly track.

win <- cilla |> arrange(t_) |> filter(t_ < min(t_) + days(25))

run_bcpa <- function(d, windowsize) {
  vt <- GetVT(MakeTrack(d$x_, d$y_, d$t_))
  set.seed(1)
  ws <- WindowSweep(vt, "V*cos(Theta)", windowsize = windowsize,
                    progress = FALSE, K = 2)
  list(vt = vt, ws = ws, cps = ChangePointSummary(ws, clusterwidth = 3))
}

b1 <- run_bcpa(win, windowsize = 50)
nrow(b1$cps$phases)
#> [1] 29


plot(b1$vt$T.POSIX, b1$vt$V * cos(b1$vt$Theta), type = "l", col = "grey60",
     xlab = "", ylab = "V cos(θ)  (m/h)", main = "Cilla: BCPA change points")
abline(v = b1$cps$breaks$middle.POSIX, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)







Your turn
6a. Rerun with windowsize = 30. 6b. Resample to 3-hourly and rerun with a window covering the same time (17 fixes ≈ 50 hours). 6c. How many change points survive both analyses?






NoteSolution






b1_30 <- run_bcpa(win, windowsize = 30)

win_3h <- win |> track_resample(rate = hours(3), tolerance = minutes(15))
b3_17  <- run_bcpa(win_3h, windowsize = 17)
b3_50  <- run_bcpa(win_3h, windowsize = 50)

data.frame(
  analysis = c("hourly, 50-fix window", "hourly, 30-fix window",
               "3-hourly, 17-fix window (~50 h)", "3-hourly, 50-fix window (~150 h)"),
  phases = c(nrow(b1$cps$phases), nrow(b1_30$cps$phases),
             nrow(b3_17$cps$phases), nrow(b3_50$cps$phases))
)
#>                           analysis phases
#> 1            hourly, 50-fix window     29
#> 2            hourly, 30-fix window     38
#> 3  3-hourly, 17-fix window (~50 h)     29
#> 4 3-hourly, 50-fix window (~150 h)     19

The count moves with every choice you make. The honest question is not “how many phases?” but “which change points are robust?”:

cp_1h <- b1$cps$breaks$middle.POSIX
cp_3h <- b3_17$cps$breaks$middle.POSIX

matched <- vapply(cp_1h, \(tt) any(abs(difftime(cp_3h, tt, units = "hours")) <= 6),
                  logical(1))
c(hourly_change_points = length(cp_1h),
  also_found_at_3h_within_6h = sum(matched),
  share_robust = round(mean(matched), 2))
#>       hourly_change_points also_found_at_3h_within_6h 
#>                      28.00                      21.00 
#>               share_robust 
#>                       0.75

About three quarters of the hourly change points reappear within six hours in the 3-hourly analysis. Those are the ones worth interpreting as changes in the buffalo’s behaviour. The remaining quarter appear only at one resolution: treat them as properties of the window and the sampling until shown otherwise.

title: Practical 4 — Quantifying movement
text:
Self-check

Turning angles of a track sampled every 6 hours are close to uniform. What does this tell you?

The animal moves at random
Directional persistence operates on a shorter timescale than 6 hours
The resampling introduced an error
GPS error dominates


Persistence is a short-term property: over six hours the animal has changed activity several times, so one step’s direction says little about the next. That is a statement about the timescale of the behaviour relative to your sampling, not about the animal being random.



A disperser model fits a known migrant best. Most likely cause?

The animal changed strategy
The data cover only part of the annual cycle
AIC is unreliable for non-linear models
The CRS is wrong


A migration observed only on the way out is a single step up in NSD — the disperser curve. Classify only complete cycles, and check the dates of your data before interpreting any strategy.

raw <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>

Task 1b — The same trajectory as an ltraj

adehabitatLT stores a trajectory as a list of bursts, with the step descriptors already computed.

cilla <- trk |> filter(id == "Cilla")

ltr <- as.ltraj(xy = as.data.frame(cilla[, c("x_", "y_")]),
                date = cilla$t_, id = "Cilla")
ltr

#> 2 2005-07-14 05:35:00  3943.3528 7200 179194206  2.3910145 1.4903537

dist is step length (m), dt the interval (s), R2n the squared distance from the first fix (we use it in Session 4), and rel.angle the turning angle.
Your turn
1c. Compute step lengths and turning angles with amt and check they agree with the ltraj columns.






NoteSolution






st_cilla <- cilla |> steps()
c(amt_median_sl = median(st_cilla$sl_),
  ltraj_median_dist = median(ld(ltr)$dist, na.rm = TRUE))
#>     amt_median_sl ltraj_median_dist 
#>          149.4087          149.4087

# amt's ta_ and adehabitat's rel.angle are the same quantity
a <- st_cilla$ta_[-1]
b <- ld(ltr)$rel.angle[2:nrow(st_cilla)]
both <- !is.na(a) & !is.na(b)

naive    <- max(abs(a[both] - b[both]))                       # plain subtraction
circular <- max(abs(atan2(sin(a[both] - b[both]),             # difference on
                          cos(a[both] - b[both]))))           # the circle
c(compared = sum(both), naive_max_diff = naive, circular_max_diff = circular,
  NA_in_amt = sum(is.na(a)), NA_in_adehabitat = sum(is.na(b)))
#>          compared    naive_max_diff circular_max_diff         NA_in_amt 
#>      3.516000e+03      6.283185e+00      8.881784e-16      1.000000e+01 
#>  NA_in_adehabitat 
#>      5.000000e+00

Two lessons in one table.
Angles are circular. Plain subtraction reports a maximum difference of exactly 2π — one package wrote a U-turn as +π, the other as −π, which are the same direction. Measured on the circle the difference is zero. Never compare, average or subtract angles as ordinary numbers.
Undefined angles. The packages disagree on how many turns to leave undefined around zero-length steps: a step of 0 m has no direction, so the turn into or out of it cannot be computed. amt blanks more of them than adehabitatLT does. Worth knowing before you compare turning-angle distributions across packages.
Otherwise: same numbers, different containers. Use whichever the next analysis needs: ltraj for first-passage time and Brownian bridges (Sessions 4 and 6), amt for resampling and step selection.

gaps <- trk |>

text:
Task 3 — Hunt the speed outliers
First, look. Then delete.

steps_raw <- trk |>
  group_by(id) |>
  arrange(t_, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    dt_h = as.numeric(difftime(t_, lag(t_), units = "hours")),
    dist_m = sqrt((x_ - lag(x_))^2 + (y_ - lag(y_))^2),
    speed_kmh = (dist_m / 1000) / dt_h
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(!is.na(speed_kmh))

sum(steps_raw$speed_kmh > 15)

  slice_max(speed_kmh, n = 10) |>
  transmute(id, t_, dt_min = round(dt_h * 60, 1),
            dist_m = round(dist_m), speed_kmh = round(speed_kmh))

#>    id     t_                  dt_min dist_m speed_kmh
#>  * <chr>  <dttm>               <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
#>  1 Toni   2006-04-20 19:10:00     60  63103        63
#>  2 Toni   2006-04-20 18:10:00     61  63067        62
