The worst offenders have tiny time gaps, not large distances — a couple of hundred metres over a minute or two. These are near-duplicate transmissions that survived the exact-duplicate filter.
Confirm it across all the fast steps:

fast <- steps_raw |> filter(speed_kmh > 15)
summary(fast$dt_h * 60)     # minutes
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>    60.0    60.0    60.5    60.5    61.0    61.0
summary(fast$dist_m)        # metres
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   16804   17235   40223   40088   63076   63103


plot(steps_raw$dt_h * 60, steps_raw$speed_kmh, log = "xy",
     pch = 16, cex = 0.25, col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.25),
     xlab = "Time gap (minutes, log)", ylab = "Speed km/h (log)",
     main = "Fast steps are short-interval steps")
abline(h = 15, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)







The diagonal edge is the signature: apparent speed is bounded by (GPS error)/dt, so as dt shrinks, apparent speed explodes. This is a time problem masquerading as a speed problem — and deleting the “fast” fixes would remove perfectly good locations.
The correct remedy is to resample onto a regular grid, which is Task 4.

title: Practical 3 — From fixes to trajectories
text:
Task 4 — Resample into bursts
This is where almost everyone writes a silent bug. Try the obvious thing first.

# The "obvious" pipeline — grouped by individual
naive <- trk |>
  group_by(id) |>
  track_resample(rate = hours(1), tolerance = minutes(10)) |>
  filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3) |>
  ungroup()

nrow(trk)
#> [1] 24663
nrow(naive)
#> [1] 10395
naive |> count(id, name = "kept")
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   id      kept
#>   <chr>  <int>
#> 1 Cilla   2731
#> 2 Gabs    1921
#> 3 Mvubu    166
#> 4 Pepper   644
#> 5 Queen   1741
#> 6 Toni    3192







Importanttrack_resample() does not respect group_by()



Look at the per-animal counts. Mvubu goes from 2,572 fixes to a couple of hundred — but Mvubu’s data are fine: 98.8% of that animal’s intervals are within 10 minutes of one hour.
track_resample() walks the rows in time order and builds one grid across everything you hand it. With six animals interleaved, fixes from animal B fall between the grid points of animal A, and most of the track is discarded. No error. No warning. Just a much smaller dataset.


The documented amt idiom is to split, resample each animal separately, and recombine:

library(tidyr)

trk_hr <- trk |>
  nest(data = -id) |>
  mutate(data = lapply(data, \(d) {
    d |>
      track_resample(rate = hours(1), tolerance = minutes(10)) |>
      filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3)
  })) |>
  unnest(cols = data)

nrow(trk_hr)
#> [1] 22828


trk |> count(id, name = "before") |>
  left_join(naive   |> count(id, name = "grouped_WRONG"), by = "id") |>
  left_join(trk_hr  |> count(id, name = "nested_right"), by = "id") |>
  mutate(pct_kept = round(100 * nested_right / before, 1))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   id     before grouped_WRONG nested_right pct_kept
#> * <chr>   <int>         <int>        <int>    <dbl>
#> 1 Cilla    3528          2731         3518     99.7
#> 2 Gabs     3670          1921         3562     97.1
#> 3 Mvubu    2572           166         2544     98.9
#> 4 Pepper   4571           644         3086     67.5
#> 5 Queen    4545          1741         4354     95.8
#> 6 Toni     5777          3192         5764     99.8

Now we keep ~93% of the fixes, which is what an hourly schedule with occasional failures should give.
Your turn
4a. Recompute speeds on the correctly resampled track. Did the problem go away? 4b. What happens if you set tolerance = minutes(1)?






NoteSolution






st <- trk_hr |> steps_by_burst()

summary(as.numeric(st$dt_, units = "mins"))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>      54      60      60      60      60      70

sp <- (st$sl_ / 1000) / as.numeric(st$dt_, units = "hours")
round(quantile(sp, c(0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, 1)), 2)
#>   50%   90%   99% 99.9%  100% 
#>  0.15  0.73  1.93  3.05 63.10
sum(sp > 15)
#> [1] 4

Every step now spans 50–70 minutes, and the time-artefact speeds are gone: the median is a few hundred metres per hour, which is what a buffalo does.
But a handful of steps remain absurdly fast. These are different animals entirely — look at them:

st[sp > 15, c("t1_", "sl_", "dt_")] |> head(5)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   t1_                    sl_ dt_    
#> * <dttm>               <dbl> <drtn> 
#> 1 2006-04-20 17:09:00 63067. 61 mins
#> 2 2006-04-20 18:10:00 63103. 60 mins
#> 3 2006-05-24 04:06:00 17379. 60 mins
#> 4 2006-05-24 05:06:00 16804. 61 mins

Sixty-five kilometres in an hour. That is not a short time gap; it is a genuine spatial outlier — a corrupt fix that teleported the animal and back. Now that every step spans the same interval, a fast step really does mean a long distance, and a speed filter finally does what you meant it to do.

plot(as.numeric(st$dt_, units = "mins"), sp, log = "y", pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
     col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.3),
     xlab = "Step duration (minutes)", ylab = "Speed km/h (log)",
     main = "After resampling: fast = far, not brief")
abline(h = 15, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)







Compare this with the plot in Task 3: the diagonal artefact edge has gone, and what is left above the line is a small, isolated cluster of real errors.

tight <- trk |>
  nest(data = -id) |>
  mutate(data = lapply(data, \(d) d |>
    track_resample(rate = hours(1), tolerance = minutes(1)) |>
    filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3))) |>
  unnest(cols = data)

c(tolerance_10min = nrow(trk_hr), tolerance_1min = nrow(tight))
#> tolerance_10min  tolerance_1min 
#>           22828           21903

A tight tolerance discards fixes that arrived a few minutes late — real data you would rather keep. A loose one lets “hourly” steps range from 40 to 80 minutes, weakening every step-length comparison. 5–10% of the interval is a reasonable compromise; state whichever you chose.

title: Practical 3 — From fixes to trajectories
Practical 3 — From fixes to trajectories
text:
Task 6 — Interpolation is not resampling
adehabitatLT::redisltraj() also produces a regular hourly series — by inventing positions.

cilla_ltr <- as.ltraj(xy = as.data.frame(cilla[, c("x_", "y_")]),
                      date = cilla$t_, id = "Cilla")
interp <- redisltraj(cilla_ltr, 3600, type = "time")

selected <- trk_hr |> filter(id == "Cilla")

c(original_fixes = nrow(cilla),
  selected_by_track_resample = nrow(selected),
  produced_by_redisltraj = nrow(ld(interp)))
#>             original_fixes selected_by_track_resample 
#>                       3528                       3518 
#>     produced_by_redisltraj 
#>                       3522

Your turn
6a. How many of the interpolated positions coincide with a real fix? 6b. What would interpolated positions do to a step-length distribution?






NoteSolution






real_times <- cilla$t_
interp_times <- ld(interp)$date
sum(interp_times %in% real_times)
#> [1] 30
length(interp_times)
#> [1] 3522

Almost none of the “hourly” positions is an observation: redisltraj() walks along the straight lines between fixes and places a point every 3,600 seconds. Every one of those points assumes the animal moved at constant speed in a straight line between fixes.
Consequences: step lengths across a gap become artificially uniform, turning angles on interpolated stretches become exactly zero, and any model fitted to them sees a smooth, persistent animal that never existed. Use interpolation for display, never as data — or use a model that interpolates with uncertainty (ctmm, crawl), which is what Sessions 6 and 8 do.

text:
Task 7 — Day or night?
Many behaviours are diel. time_of_day() labels each fix from the sun’s position at that place and time.

cilla_tod <- selected |>
  time_of_day()

cilla_steps <- cilla_tod |>
  steps_by_burst(keep_cols = "start")

cilla_steps |>
  group_by(tod_) |>
  summarise(steps = n(), median_sl_m = round(median(sl_)),
            mean_sl_m = round(mean(sl_)))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   tod_  steps median_sl_m mean_sl_m
#>   <fct> <int>       <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 day    1801         221       347
#> 2 night  1714         104       218







NoteWhat this shows





Buffalo move further per hour by day than by night — a diel pattern you must account for before interpreting anything else about their movement. In Session 8 we let the probability of switching behavioural state depend on the time of day.

section: Task 8 — NDVI matched to the time of each fix
text:
Task 8 — NDVI matched to the time of each fix
The NDVI raster from Session 2 has two layers, a wet-season composite (2 Feb 2005) and a dry-season one (14 Sep 2005). Tell terra when each was taken, then let amt give every fix the value of the composite closest in time.

ndvi <- project(rast("data/kruger_ndvi_2005.tif"), "EPSG:32736")
time(ndvi) <- as.POSIXct(c("2005-02-02", "2005-09-14"), tz = "UTC")
ndvi
#> class       : SpatRaster
#> size        : 504, 445, 2  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 258.5037, 258.5037  (x, y)
#> extent      : 338541.4, 453575.6, 7215872, 7346158  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : WGS 84 / UTM zone 36S (EPSG:32736)
#> source(s)   : memory
#> names       : ndvi_2005_02_02, ndvi_2005_09_14
#> min values  :       -0.196056,       -0.198263
#> max values  :        0.804637,        0.583936
#> time        : 2005-02-02 00:00:00zUTC to 2005-09-14 00:00:00zUTC (2 steps)

queen <- trk |> filter(id == "Queen", year(t_) == 2005)

queen_ndvi <- queen |>
  extract_covariates_var_time(ndvi, when = "any", max_time = days(45),
                              name_covar = "ndvi")

queen_ndvi |>
  mutate(month = month(t_, label = TRUE)) |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarise(fixes = n(), with_ndvi = sum(!is.na(ndvi)),
            mean_ndvi = round(mean(ndvi, na.rm = TRUE), 3))
#> # A tibble: 9 × 4
#>   month fixes with_ndvi mean_ndvi
#>   <ord> <int>     <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 Feb     285       285     0.59 
#> 2 Mar     751       438     0.607
#> 3 Apr     646         0   NaN    
#> 4 May      73         0   NaN    
#> 5 Jun       1         0   NaN    
#> 6 Sep     319       319     0.252
#> 7 Oct     676       604     0.252
#> 8 Nov     719         0   NaN    
#> 9 Dec     737         0   NaN

Your turn
8a. Why are most months NA? 8b. What would you need to annotate the whole year?






NoteSolution





With max_time = days(45), a fix is annotated only if a composite exists within 45 days of it. We have two composites, so only February–March and September–October are covered. Everything else is honestly NA — far better than silently assigning February’s greenness to a July fix.
To annotate the whole year you need the full series: MOD13Q1 produces a composite every 16 days, 23 per year. The same MODISTools call that built this file fetches them all — it just takes longer:

library(MODISTools)
ndvi_ts <- mt_subset(product = "MOD13Q1", band = "250m_16_days_NDVI",
                     lat = -24.58, lon = 31.97, km_lr = 45, km_ab = 70,
                     start = "2005-01-01", end = "2006-12-31")
ndvi_ts <- mt_to_terra(ndvi_ts, reproject = TRUE)   # already scaled to NDVI units

Or upload the track to Movebank’s Env-DATA, which does the matching and the temporal interpolation for you. Either way, check the result with summary(): NDVI must lie between −1 and 1. If you see values in the thousands, the scale factor was not applied; if you see values a thousand times too small, it was applied twice.

title: Practical 3 — From fixes to trajectories
text:
Self-check

Which cleaning order is correct?

Speed filter → remove duplicates → resample
Remove duplicates → resample to a regular rate → inspect remaining outliers
Resample → remove duplicates → speed filter
The order does not matter


Duplicates and near-duplicates create tiny time gaps, and tiny time gaps create enormous apparent speeds. Filter on speed first and you delete good fixes for a fault that belongs to their neighbours.
Remove duplicates, then resample so that every step spans a comparable interval, and then look at what is still implausible. By that point, a genuinely fast step really is a long distance.



You pipe six animals into group_by(id) |> track_resample(rate = hours(1)) and keep 42% of your fixes. The same animals resampled one at a time keep 93%. Why?

track_resample() ignores group_by() and builds one time grid across all animals
group_by() removed the duplicate timestamps
The tolerance was too tight
42% is correct; the per-animal version double-counts


track_resample() walks the rows in time order and lays a single regular grid over whatever you give it. Hand it six interleaved animals and most fixes fall between grid points set by some other individual, so they are dropped.
It fails silently — no error, no warning, just a smaller dataset — which is what makes it dangerous. Use the nest() / lapply() / unnest() idiom so each animal gets its own grid.
The general lesson: not every function respects dplyr grouping. When a step drops far more data than you expected, check the per-group counts before you accept the result.

title: Practical 2 — The spatial survival kit
text:
Goals. Turn a CSV into an sf object; reproject it and measure distances correctly; use the vector verbs you will need all course (st_buffer, st_join, st_intersection); load real NDVI and land-cover rasters with terra and sample them at the fixes; break things on purpose; and finish with a publication-quality map.
Time: ~80 minutes. Packages: sf, terra, dplyr, ggplot2, ggspatial.
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

title: Practical 2 — The spatial survival kit
section: Task 1 — From data frame to sf
text:
Task 1 — From data frame to sf


track <- readr::read_csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(id = `individual-local-identifier`, t = timestamp,
            lon = `location-long`, lat = `location-lat`) |>
  filter(!is.na(lon), !is.na(lat)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  arrange(id, t)

fixes <- st_as_sf(track, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)
fixes

#> 10 Cilla 2005-07-14 14:35:00  31.9 -24.9   (31.857 -24.93371)
#> # ℹ 24,653 more rows

Your turn
1a. What CRS is this, in what units? 1b. What is the bounding box?






NoteSolution






st_crs(fixes)$epsg
#> [1] 4326
st_is_longlat(fixes)
#> [1] TRUE
st_bbox(fixes)
#>      xmin      ymin      xmax      ymax 
#>  31.58639 -25.16421  32.35671 -23.99802

EPSG:4326, degrees — and st_is_longlat() returning TRUE is the flag that should make you stop before computing any distance or area.

title: Practical 2 — The spatial survival kit
section: Task 2 — Reproject, and measure one distance three ways
text:
Task 2 — Reproject, and measure one distance three ways
Kruger is in UTM zone 36S, EPSG:32736.

fixes_utm <- st_transform(fixes, 32736)

queen <- fixes |> filter(id == "Queen") |> slice(1:2)
xy <- st_coordinates(queen)

wrong     <- sqrt(diff(xy[, 1])^2 + diff(xy[, 2])^2)          # "distance" in degrees
geodesic  <- st_distance(queen[1, ], queen[2, ])              # on the ellipsoid
projected <- st_distance(st_transform(queen, 32736)[1, ],
                         st_transform(queen, 32736)[2, ])     # in UTM metres

c(wrong_degrees = wrong, geodesic_m = as.numeric(geodesic),
  projected_m = as.numeric(projected))
#> wrong_degrees    geodesic_m   projected_m 
#>  2.835514e-03  3.014658e+02  3.009957e+02







NoteWhat the three numbers mean





The first is not a distance at all: it mixes degrees of longitude and latitude, which are different lengths. The other two agree to a small fraction of a percent — UTM’s distortion inside a zone is under 0.1%.
For distances either works. For kernel densities, buffers and anything involving area, project first: those methods assume a plane.

title: Practical 2 — The spatial survival kit
section: Task 3 — Vector verbs: buffer, join, intersect
text:
Task 3 — Vector verbs: buffer, join, intersect
We need polygons to overlay. Build them from the land-cover raster: for each cell, which cover type dominates?

lc <- rast("data/kruger_landcover.tif")[[c("trees", "grassland", "shrubs")]]
dominant <- which.max(lc)
levels(dominant) <- data.frame(id = 1:3, cover = c("trees", "grassland", "shrubs"))

habitat <- as.polygons(dominant, dissolve = TRUE) |>
  st_as_sf() |>
  st_transform(32736)

habitat
#> Simple feature collection with 3 features and 1 field
#> Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 337122.5 ymin: 7200872 xmax: 449667.9 ymax: 7356755
#> Projected CRS: WGS 84 / UTM zone 36S
#>       cover                       geometry
#> 1     trees MULTIPOLYGON (((387178.5 73...
#> 2 grassland MULTIPOLYGON (((411785.8 73...
#> 3    shrubs MULTIPOLYGON (((405848 7355...


st_join() — which polygon is each fix in?

fixes_hab <- st_join(fixes_utm, habitat)

fixes_hab |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(cover) |>
  mutate(share = round(n / sum(n), 3))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   cover         n share
#>   <chr>     <int> <dbl>
#> 1 grassland 24090 0.977
#> 2 shrubs      476 0.019
#> 3 trees        97 0.004


st_buffer() and st_intersection() — what is around the animal?

cilla_area <- fixes_utm |>
  filter(id == "Cilla") |>
  st_buffer(dist = 500) |>          # 500 m around every fix
  st_union()                        # one polygon: the area Cilla came near

used_hab <- st_intersection(habitat, cilla_area) |>
  mutate(km2 = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 1e6)

used_hab |> st_drop_geometry() |> select(cover, km2)
#>       cover        km2
#> 1     trees   2.424118
#> 2 grassland 221.503730
#> 3    shrubs   1.848077

Your turn
3a. Compare the habitat composition of Cilla’s area with that of the whole landscape. 3b. Why must habitat and cilla_area be projected here?






NoteSolution






study <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(habitat))
landscape <- st_intersection(habitat, study) |>
  mutate(km2 = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 1e6)

left_join(
  landscape |> st_drop_geometry() |> transmute(cover, landscape = km2 / sum(km2)),
  used_hab  |> st_drop_geometry() |> transmute(cover, cilla = km2 / sum(km2)),
  by = "cover"
) |>
  mutate(across(c(landscape, cilla), \(z) round(z, 3)),
         ratio = round(cilla / landscape, 2))
#>       cover landscape cilla ratio
#> 1     trees     0.245 0.011  0.04
#> 2 grassland     0.424 0.981  2.31
#> 3    shrubs     0.331 0.008  0.02

A ratio above 1 means Cilla’s surroundings contain more of that cover than the landscape does. This used-versus-available comparison is the seed of Session 7.
Both layers must be projected because st_buffer(dist = 500) needs metres (in degrees, 500 would be absurd) and st_area() of a union of buffers assumes a plane. sf would compute geodesic areas on 4326, but buffering in degrees produces ellipses, not circles.

title: Practical 2 — The spatial survival kit
text:
Task 4 — Rasters with terra: NDVI
data/kruger_ndvi_2005.tif holds two MODIS 16-day NDVI composites (MOD13Q1, 250 m) over the buffalo range: one from the wet season and one from the dry season of 2005.

ndvi <- rast("data/kruger_ndvi_2005.tif")
ndvi
#> class       : SpatRaster
#> size        : 481, 463, 2  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 0.002432149, 0.002432149  (x, y)
#> extent      : 31.41276, 32.53885, -25.1657, -23.99583  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : lon/lat WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)
#> source      : kruger_ndvi_2005.tif
#> names       : ndvi_2005_02_02, ndvi_2005_09_14
#> min values  :       -0.198494,       -0.198628
#> max values  :        0.852371,        0.599399


plot(ndvi, col = hcl.colors(50, "Greens", rev = TRUE), range = c(0, 0.9))







Your turn
4a. What is the resolution in metres? What CRS is it in? 4b. Extract both NDVI layers at every buffalo fix.






NoteSolution






crs(ndvi, describe = TRUE)$code
#> [1] "4326"
res(ndvi)
#> [1] 0.002432149 0.002432149
round(res(ndvi) * c(111320 * cos(24.6 * pi / 180), 111320))   # approx metres
#> [1] 246 271

About 230 m east–west and 230 m north–south — MODIS’s 250 m product, delivered here in longitude/latitude.

fixes$ndvi_wet <- terra::extract(ndvi[["ndvi_2005_02_02"]], vect(fixes))[, 2]
fixes$ndvi_dry <- terra::extract(ndvi[["ndvi_2005_09_14"]], vect(fixes))[, 2]

summary(st_drop_geometry(fixes)[, c("ndvi_wet", "ndvi_dry")])
#>     ndvi_wet         ndvi_dry     
#>  Min.   :0.2920   Min.   :0.1570  
#>  1st Qu.:0.4985   1st Qu.:0.2108  
#>  Median :0.5859   Median :0.2391  
#>  Mean   :0.5674   Mean   :0.2401  
#>  3rd Qu.:0.6426   3rd Qu.:0.2656  
#>  Max.   :0.7435   Max.   :0.3927  
#>  NAs    :1        NAs    :1

The same places are far greener in February than in September. Which value belongs to which fix depends on when the fix was taken — Session 3 does that matching properly.

title: Practical 2 — The spatial survival kit
text:
Task 5 — Break it on purpose
Two silent failures worth recognising for the rest of your career.
A bare coordinate matrix has no CRS

ndvi_utm <- project(ndvi, "EPSG:32736")

# Both objects carry a CRS: terra reprojects for you, with a warning
ok <- terra::extract(ndvi_utm[[1]], vect(fixes))
mean(is.na(ok[, 2]))
#> [1] 4.054657e-05

# A bare matrix carries none: degrees are read as metres
bad <- terra::extract(ndvi_utm[[1]], st_coordinates(fixes))
mean(is.na(bad[, 1]))
#> [1] 1

Every value NA, no error, no warning. Keep coordinates in objects that carry their CRS.

extract(buffer = ) is ignored for points

at_fix   <- terra::extract(ndvi[[1]], vect(fixes))[, 2]
buf_2000 <- terra::extract(ndvi[[1]], vect(fixes), buffer = 2000,
                           fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)[, 2]
identical(at_fix, buf_2000)
#> [1] TRUE

The “2 km mean” is the at-fix value, unchanged. Build buffer polygons yourself:

buf_poly <- st_buffer(fixes_utm, 2000) |> st_transform(4326) |> vect()
buf_2000 <- terra::extract(ndvi[[1]], buf_poly, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)[, 2]

c(sd_at_fix = sd(at_fix, na.rm = TRUE), sd_2km_mean = sd(buf_2000, na.rm = TRUE))
#>   sd_at_fix sd_2km_mean 
#>  0.09203145  0.08682538







ImportantThe habit



When an argument is supposed to change the answer, check that it did. identical() costs one line.
Note also what smoothing does: the 2 km mean has less variance than the at-fix value. Here the reduction is modest, because savanna greenness varies mostly at scales larger than 2 km; for a patchier covariate it can be large. Either way, smoothing shrinks the contrast between used and available places. The buffer radius is a hypothesis about perception — choose it from biology, not from whichever radius gives the smallest p-value.

title: Practical 2 — The spatial survival kit
section: Task 6 — Mini-challenge: a map worth publishing
text:
Task 6 — Mini-challenge: a map worth publishing

library(ggspatial)

ndvi_df <- as.data.frame(ndvi_utm[["ndvi_2005_02_02"]], xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
names(ndvi_df)[3] <- "ndvi"

paths <- fixes_utm |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(do_union = FALSE) |>
  st_cast("LINESTRING")

# Frame the map on where the animals are (robust to a stray fix), plus a margin
xy <- st_coordinates(fixes_utm)
lims_x <- quantile(xy[, 1], c(0.001, 0.999)) + c(-4000, 4000)
lims_y <- quantile(xy[, 2], c(0.001, 0.999)) + c(-4000, 4000)

ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = ndvi_df, aes(x, y, fill = ndvi)) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = hcl.colors(9, "Greens", rev = TRUE),
                       limits = c(0, 0.9), name = "NDVI\nFeb 2005") +
  geom_sf(data = paths, aes(colour = id), linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = NULL) +
  annotation_scale(location = "bl", width_hint = 0.25) +
  annotation_north_arrow(location = "tr", style = north_arrow_minimal()) +
  coord_sf(crs = 32736, xlim = lims_x, ylim = lims_y, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "African buffalo in Kruger National Park",
       subtitle = "GPS tracks over wet-season greenness",
       caption = "Tracks: Movebank (Getz et al.). NDVI: MODIS MOD13Q1, 2 Feb 2005.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank(), legend.position = "right")













ImportantLook at Toni’s track



One straight line leaves the frame towards the north-east. That is a single corrupt fix more than 60 km away — the buffalo did not go there and back in an hour. A good map shows you problems in the data before any model does; Session 3 removes this fix properly.








TipTo hand in



Your own version of this map, as a PNG at print resolution (ggsave("map.png", width = 17, height = 15, units = "cm", dpi = 300)), plus the .qmd that makes it. It must have: a projected CRS, a scale bar, a legend with units, a caption crediting the data, and colours that survive greyscale printing. Choose a different layer or animal from the one above.

title: Practical 2 — The spatial survival kit
text:
Self-check

st_crs(x) <- 32736 on an object whose coordinates are longitude/latitude. What have you done?

Reprojected the data to UTM 36S
Mislabelled the data — the numbers are unchanged but now claimed to be metres
Nothing; sf ignores invalid assignments
Produced an error


Assigning a CRS only writes a label. 31.8 and −24.5 are now read as metres from the UTM 36S origin — a point off West Africa. It fails silently, which is what makes it dangerous. st_transform() changes coordinates.



You st_join() 20,000 fixes to a habitat layer and get back 20,412 rows. Why?

st_join() duplicates the last row
Some fixes fall in more than one polygon (overlaps, or exactly on a shared boundary)
The CRSs differ
It is a bug in sf


st_join() is a spatial left join: one output row for every match. A point on a shared boundary, or inside overlapping polygons, matches twice. Always compare row counts before and after a join, and use largest = TRUE (for polygons) or clean the polygon layer so it tiles without overlaps.

title: Practical 1 — First contact with a GPS track
text:
Task 1 — Load the track

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)

raw <- read_csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz", show_col_types = FALSE)

dim(raw)
#> [1] 28410    18
names(raw)[1:6]
#> [1] "event-id"                   "visible"                   
#> [3] "timestamp"                  "location-long"             
#> [5] "location-lat"               "behavioural-classification"

Two things to notice. read_csv() keeps Movebank’s hyphenated column names, so you need backticks to refer to them. And it has already parsed timestamp as a date-time:

class(raw$timestamp)
#> [1] "POSIXct" "POSIXt"
tz(raw$timestamp)
#> [1] "UTC"

Tidy it into the four columns every movement analysis needs:

track <- raw |>
  transmute(
    id  = `individual-local-identifier`,
    t   = timestamp,
    lon = `location-long`,
    lat = `location-lat`
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(lon), !is.na(lat)) |>
  arrange(id, t)

track
#> # A tibble: 28,410 × 4
#>    id    t                     lon   lat
#>    <chr> <dttm>              <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1 Cilla 2005-07-14 04:35:00  31.8 -25.1
#>  2 Cilla 2005-07-14 05:35:00  31.9 -25.0
#>  3 Cilla 2005-07-14 07:35:00  31.9 -24.9

Common causes of long gaps:


Battery — schedules that deliberately pause, or a collar running flat

Habitat — dense canopy, gorges and burrows block the satellites

Collar orientation — an animal lying on the antenna

Data transfer — the data exist on the collar but were never downloaded

Mortality or drop-off — the collar keeps reporting the same place, or stops

The first three are the ones that bias analyses: they are not random, they depend on where the animal is and what it is doing.

text:
Self-check

You compute diff(t) on a data frame you forgot to sort by time. What do you get?

An error
A mixture of positive and negative intervals, and nonsense summaries
Correct intervals — diff() sorts internally
All zeros


diff() subtracts each element from the next, in the order given. Out of order, you get negative time differences, and any speed computed from them is garbage — often silently, because summary() still returns numbers. Always arrange(id, t) before any step calculation.



A collar programmed for hourly fixes returns 14,000 fixes over exactly two years. Roughly what was the fix success rate?

~100%
~80%
~50%
Impossible to say without the DOP values


Two years of hourly attempts is 2 × 365 × 24 ≈ 17,520. 14,000 / 17,520 ≈ 80%, a fairly typical figure for a large mammal in mixed habitat. And the 20% that failed is not noise if failures concentrate in closed habitat.

section: Movement is the link between an animal and its environment
text:
Movement is the link between an animal and its environment
Almost every process a conservation biologist cares about is a movement process in disguise:


Gene flow — dispersal distances set population connectivity
Disease spread — contact rates are an outcome of where animals go
Population persistence — can individuals reach the next patch?
Human–wildlife conflict — where do animals and people overlap, and when?
Protected-area design — a reserve that does not contain the movements it was drawn for does not work
Climate response — range shifts are dispersal events, one individual at a time 


If you cannot describe how an organism moves, you cannot predict how it will respond to a changing landscape.

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
text:
The movement ecology paradigm
Nathan et al. (2008) reduced the whole field to four questions about every movement path:


Why move? — the internal state. Hunger, thirst, reproduction, fear. The motivation.
How to move? — the motion capacity. Legs, wings, fins; the biomechanical envelope.
When and where to move? — the navigation capacity. Memory, senses, cues, orientation.
What external factors? — the environment. Landscape, weather, predators, other individuals, people. 


\(U_t = f(\Omega, \Phi, r_t, w_t)\) — the observed path is the joint outcome of all four. This is why a track is hard to interpret: many different combinations produce similar-looking paths.

text:
Our spine for eight weeks

Each session opens with this diagram, lit up where that session’s methods speak. Tracking data record only the bottom box. Every method in this course is an attempt to reason upwards from the path to the boxes above it.

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
text:
Why move? The ecological drivers


Foraging — resources are patchy and deplete; staying costs as much as leaving
Dispersal — leaving the natal area: avoids inbreeding and competition with kin
Migration — seasonal, round-trip tracking of resources across large distances
Predator avoidance — moving away from risk, or towards refuges
Reproduction — finding mates, defending territories, provisioning young 


These map onto different scales of movement: foraging steps in minutes, dispersal once in a lifetime, migration once a year. The same animal does all of them — which is why one trajectory usually hides several processes.
crumbs: Slides — Why animals move, how we watch them

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
text:
Movement is a trade-off
Every movement decision balances gain against cost:


Energy — travelling costs calories; a richer patch further away may not pay
Risk — the best food is often where predators are; the landscape of fear (Laundré et al. 2001) can matter as much as the landscape of food
Information — exploring costs now but may pay later
Time — a day spent travelling is a day not spent feeding or breeding 


When a model says an animal “selects” a habitat, it is summarising the net outcome of all these trade-offs. Sessions 7 and 8 are about disentangling them.

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
text:
Quiz

After wolves returned to Yellowstone, elk in wolf-rich areas made less use of aspen stands, a key forage (Fortin et al. 2005). Assuming the forage itself did not change, which component of the paradigm explains the shift?

Motion capacity
Navigation capacity
External factors — acting through the animals’ internal state (fear)
None; this is a habitat-quality effect


Forage did not change, so the habitat itself did not change. What changed was predation risk — an external factor — which altered the elk’s internal state and therefore the trade-off between food and safety. This is the landscape of fear idea.
It also shows why the four components cannot be read separately: the same external change works through the animal’s internal state. It is also why a habitat-selection model fitted before and after wolf reintroduction would give different coefficients for the same, unchanged vegetation.

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
text:
Lagrangian vs Eulerian


Lagrangian
Follow the individual.
Telemetry, biologging, mark-recapture.
“Where did animal #7 go?”
Gives you the process: the sequence of decisions.

Eulerian
Watch a fixed place.
Camera traps, transects, counts, eDNA.
“How many animals passed this point?”
Gives you the pattern: density in space.


This course is almost entirely Lagrangian — but remember the two are linked: a distribution is what you get when you integrate movement over time.

text:
Vocabulary — get this right now







Term
Meaning




Fix (or relocation)
One estimated location with a timestamp. The atom of everything.


Track / trajectory
An ordered sequence of fixes for one individual


Burst
A stretch of a track with regular sampling and no big gaps


Step
The straight segment between two consecutive fixes


Step length (SL)
Distance of a step. Note: not distance travelled


Turning angle (TA)
Change of direction between consecutive steps


Fix rate / sampling interval
How often the tag tries to locate


Fix success rate
Fraction of attempts that produced a location


Deployment
One tag, on one animal, over one period





A track is not the path the animal walked. It is a sample of that path. Everything between two fixes is an assumption.

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
text:
Quiz

A GPS collar is set to attempt a fix every hour. Over one day it produces 18 locations. The straight-line distances between consecutive fixes sum to 4.1 km. Which statements are true?

The animal travelled 4.1 km that day
The animal travelled at least 4.1 km that day
The fix success rate was 75%
The 6 missing fixes can be safely ignored


4.1 km is a lower bound: the animal’s real path between fixes is at least as long as the straight line, and usually much longer. Summed step length is scale-dependent — sample twice as often and it grows.
18/24 = 75% success. And the missing fixes are the opposite of ignorable: GPS failures are not random. Fixes fail under canopy, in gorges, in dense cover — exactly the habitats an animal may be selecting. Missing data are themselves an ecological signal.

A Passive Integrated Transponder (PIT)

Genetic tagging

Species and locations where genetic tagging has delivered demographic insight (after Lamb et al. 2019)Hair snags, scats, feathers: the animal is never handled. Biased towards mid-to-large mobile mammals, because that is where the money and the conflict are.

text:
VHF radio-telemetry





Implanted transmitter, Chilabothrus chrysogaster






Tracking on foot with a Yagi antenna



The tag emits a pulse; you find it. A location comes from homing in or from triangulation of ≥2 bearings. Tags go down to 0.2 g — nothing else reaches insects and the smallest bats.

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
text:
What triangulation actually costs you


Each bearing has error; the location error is the intersection polygon of two noisy bearings, and it grows fast with distance
Data arrive when a human is in the field — so nights, storms and weekends are systematically under-sampled
A few dozen to a few hundred fixes per animal, unevenly spaced
Cheap tags, expensive fieldwork 


The bat dataset we will use in Session 3 is exactly this: 17 individuals, 1,740 fixes in total, wildly irregular. Most methods in this course assume regular sampling. Part of your training is learning to say “not with these data”.

GPS: trilateration


The GPS constellation
Each satellite broadcasts its position and a very precise time
Distance to a satellite = (signal travel time) × c
3 satellites fix a position in principle; a 4th is needed to solve the receiver’s clock error — and more give altitude and redundancy

text:
GPS in practice, on an animal


What you get

Horizontal error typically 5–30 m under open sky
A quality flag: number of satellites, DOP (dilution of precision), 2D vs 3D fix
Optional altitude, speed, temperature, activity

What it costs

A cold start (no recent almanac) can take minutes and drain the battery
Canopy, canyons, burrows and water block the signal
Energy scales with fix rate — this is the central design trade-off

section: Getting the data off the animal
text:
Getting the data off the animal


Store-on-board — cheapest, best battery use, but you must recapture the animal. Lose the animal, lose everything.
VHF/UHF download — get close, pull the data over the air
GSM / SMS — near-live data wherever there is mobile coverage. Fails in exactly the remote places you care about.
Iridium / Argos uplink — global, live, expensive, small data volumes
Drop-off collars — timed or remotely triggered release, then go and find the collar. Elegant, and one more thing that can fail. 


Ask “how will I get the data back?” before you buy the tags. This is the question most first projects get wrong.

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
section: Argos, geolocators, and the aquatic world
text:
Argos, geolocators, and the aquatic world


Argos
Satellites measure the Doppler shift of the tag’s transmission.
Error classes 3 → B: ~250 m to >10 km.
Global, works at sea, decades of history. Still standard for sea turtles, seabirds, pinnipeds.

Geolocators (GLS)
Log light level. Day length → latitude; time of local noon → longitude.
Error 100–200 km. Useless near equinox.
But: ~0.3 g. For small migratory birds it is the only option.

Acoustic telemetry
Tag pings; fixed hydrophones listen.
You get detections at receivers, not positions — a network problem, not a trajectory problem.
Fish, sharks, invertebrates.

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
section: Biologging: sensors that are not locations
text:
Biologging: sensors that are not locations


Tri-axial accelerometers — the workhorse. At 10–50 Hz you can classify feeding, resting, flying, and estimate energy expenditure (ODBA)
Magnetometers + gyroscopes — heading and body rotation; combined with accelerometers gives dead reckoning: a fine-scale path between GPS fixes
Pressure / depth — dive profiles
Temperature, heart rate, gut temperature — physiology in the wild
Proximity tags — who was near whom, and for how long: social networks 


The frontier is not more locations. It is locations plus sensors: knowing where and what the animal was doing there. Session 8 is the statistical version of this question when all you have is the trajectory.

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
text:
Archival tags and camera traps


Archival tags
Store everything on board — depth, temperature, light, acceleration — for months or years. No transmission, so tiny and long-lived.
The catch: you only get the data if you get the tag back. Pop-up archival tags on fish detach and float to the surface to transmit a summary.

Camera traps
Eulerian, not Lagrangian: they watch a place, not an animal.
But they are the natural complement to tracking — who else uses the places your collared animals use, when, and how often? Occupancy and spatial capture–recapture models connect the two worlds.

text:
Quiz

You must study the migratory route of a 22 g passerine that breeds in Italy and winters somewhere in sub-Saharan Africa. Individuals return to the same nest box each spring. Which technology?

GPS/GSM collar
Light-level geolocator
Argos PTT
VHF radio-telemetry


The 5% rule decides it: the tag should stay under ~5% of body mass, so ~1.1 g here. That excludes GPS/GSM and Argos PTTs outright. VHF has no transcontinental range.
A geolocator weighs a few tenths of a gram. Its 100–200 km error would be useless for home-range work but is irrelevant for a 4,000 km migration.
And crucially: geolocators are store-on-board, so the whole design depends on the birds’ nest-box philopatry — you must recapture them. That is not a detail, it is the study.

text:
Tag effects are real


The 3–5% rule (tag ≤ 3% of body mass for flying animals, ≤ 5% for terrestrial ones) is a convention, not a finding. Portugal & White (2018) showed miniaturisation has not made published studies lighter relative to body mass — researchers just tag smaller animals.
For flying and diving animals, drag and shape matter more than mass. A streamlined 3% package can beat a bluff 1.5% one.
Documented effects: reduced breeding success, higher energy expenditure, altered diving, changed social status, injury at the attachment site.
Effects are often delayed — and studies are rarely designed to detect them. 


A tagged animal is, to some degree, a modified animal. The honest position is to minimise, measure and report the effect — not to assume it away.

Ethics and permits: the checklist


Is the question worth it? Would existing data answer it?
3 Rs — replace, reduce, refine. The smallest sample that can answer the question.
Ethics approval and national/regional permits, before fieldwork. In Italy: ISPRA and regional authorisations; EU Directive 2010/63 where applicable.
Capture and handling protocol, anaesthesia where required, trained personnel.
Attachment — weak links and planned drop-offs so nothing is worn forever.
Data sensitivity — for poached species, publishing exact coordinates can be lethal. Movebank supports embargo and coarsening.
Report the effects you observed, including the animals you lost.

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
text:
Quiz

Which of these is the strongest argument for choosing a 30-minute fix interval over a 5-minute one, for a study of buffalo habitat selection?

30-minute data are more accurate
It extends the deployment over a whole year, capturing seasonal variation
Statistical software cannot handle 5-minute data
30 minutes is the standard for ungulates


Fix interval is a battery decision, and therefore a decision about how long you observe. 5-minute data over six weeks and 30-minute data over a year answer different questions — and for seasonal habitat selection, the year wins.
Accuracy per fix does not change with rate. Software is not the constraint. And “it’s the standard” is never a reason — it is a description of what other people’s batteries could manage.
The real cost: coarse sampling truncates the step-length distribution. You will see this bite in Sessions 4 and 7.

text:
The modifiable temporal unit problem
The spatial version is famous in geography (Openshaw 1984): results change with the size of the spatial units you aggregate into. Tracking has its own temporal version.


Path length shrinks as the interval grows — every straight segment cuts corners the animal actually walked
Speed is really distance per interval: the same animal is “slower” when sampled more coarsely
Tortuosity and turning angles change — fine sampling shows wiggles, coarse sampling shows randomness
Behaviours shorter than the interval become invisible 


There is no “true” speed or step length independent of the fix interval. Choose the interval from the question, and never compare metrics across studies sampled at different rates.

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
text:
Designing a deployment
Four numbers you fix before the first capture:


Fix interval — set by the fastest behaviour you need to resolve
Duration — set by the slowest process (seasonal selection needs a year)
Number of animals — set by the population question; individuals vary
Battery — the budget that forces 1 × 2 × 3 into a compromise 


Interval × duration × number of animals ≈ constant for a given budget. A study of foraging decisions and a study of seasonal range shifts need different collars, or at least different schedules.

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
text:
Quiz

You compute a buffalo’s daily travel distance from hourly fixes and get 4 km. A colleague using the same collars set to fix every 5 minutes reports 9 km for the same population. What is the most likely explanation?

The colleague’s collars were less accurate
Finer sampling captures more of the path’s tortuosity, so summed distance grows
The populations behave differently
Hourly fixes over-estimate distance


Summed step length is a lower bound on the distance travelled, and the bound tightens as sampling gets finer: every hourly step cuts across the wiggles that 5-minute fixes capture. More than doubling is entirely normal.
There is a second, smaller effect working the other way: at very fine intervals GPS error adds spurious zig-zag, inflating distance. That is why the “right” interval is not simply “as fine as possible”.
Neither 4 km nor 9 km is the daily distance. Each is a daily distance at a given sampling interval, and must be reported that way.

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
section: Bias 1 — Fix success is not random
text:
Bias 1 — Fix success is not random


GPS fixes fail under dense canopy, in steep terrain, in burrows, underwater
So the fixes you have are biased towards open habitat
Then you fit a habitat-selection model and conclude the animal prefers open habitat
You have measured your collar, not your animal 


Fixes are missing because of the covariate you are modelling. This is missing-not-at-random, the nastiest kind. Mitigation: stationary test collars in each habitat type, and model fix success explicitly.
crumbs: Slides — Why animals move, how we watch them

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
text:
Bias 2 — Location error is structured


Error is not independent white noise: it is correlated in time and correlated with habitat
A bad fix can place an animal hundreds of metres away, producing an implausible step out and an implausible step back — a spike
Naïvely, that spike inflates your speed distribution and your home range
Filtering on speed is the standard fix, but a threshold that is too aggressive deletes real fast movement 

Keep the DOP / satellite-count columns. They are your evidence about which fixes to distrust. We use them in Session 3.
crumbs: Slides — Why animals move, how we watch them

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
text:
Bias 3 — The sample of animals


Tagged animals are the ones you could catch: often bolder, often in accessible places, often adults, often one sex
Sample sizes are small — 6 buffalo, 1 vulture. Individual variation is large, and \(n=1\) tells you about that individual
Tags fail unevenly: animals in rough habitat lose collars more often, so late in a study your sample has drifted
Publication bias: dispersal studies report the animals that were found 


Three questions for every tracking paper you read, including yours: Which animals? Which fixes? What is missing, and why?

title: Why animals move, and how we watch them
text:
Quiz

A study reports that collared deer “avoid dense forest”, based on GPS collars with an overall fix success of 62%. What is the first thing you should check?

Whether the sample size was large enough
Whether fix success itself differed between forest and open habitat
Whether the collars were calibrated
Whether the study was peer-reviewed


A 38% failure rate is enormous, and canopy is the classic cause of GPS failure. If the collar fails more often under trees, forest locations are under-represented in the data by construction — and “avoidance” is an artefact of the instrument.
Sample size does not help: more collars with the same bias give you a more precise wrong answer. The standard remedy is stationary test collars deployed across habitat types to estimate habitat-specific fix rates, then weight or model accordingly.

Where we are going

This is the standalone “intro to spatial R” session. It is worth having even if you never analyse another track.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
Vector and raster


Vector
Discrete objects with coordinates.

Point — a fix, a nest, a trap
Line — a trajectory, a river, a road
Polygon — a home range, a park boundary, a lake

Each object carries an attribute table.
Exact geometry, arbitrary precision.

Raster
A regular grid of cells, each with a value.

Elevation, NDVI, temperature, land cover
Defined by origin, cell size, number of rows/cols, CRS

Continuous surfaces, fixed resolution.
Fast maths, no notion of individual objects.



Movement analysis is nearly always points (or steps) sampling rasters. That one sentence describes Sessions 3 and 7.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
The same place, both ways

Cilla’s fixes, one week of her track and her range as vectors; the terrain under them as a raster.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
Choosing the model







Question
Model




Where exactly was the animal at 08:00?
Vector (point)


What is the NDVI there?
Raster, sampled at that point


What is the park boundary?
Vector (polygon)


How far is the nearest river?
Raster (a distance surface) or vector + distance computation


How much forest within 500 m?
Raster, summarised in a buffer




The same reality can be either. A river is a line if you care about its course, and a distance-to-river raster if you care about how far the animal is from it. Choose by the operation you need, not by what the thing “is”.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
The problem
The Earth is a lumpy ellipsoid. Maps and computer screens are flat. Getting from one to the other requires choices, and every choice distorts something.

A CRS answers three questions:

What shape is the Earth? — the ellipsoid (e.g. WGS84, GRS80)
How is that shape tied to the actual planet? — the datum
How do we flatten it? — the projection (or none, if we keep angles)

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
Geographic coordinates

Longitude and latitude are angles, not distancesLatitude: angle north/south of the equator. Longitude: angle east/west of Greenwich. Units are degrees. This is what every GPS and every Movebank file gives you — usually WGS84, EPSG:4326.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
section: Why you cannot do arithmetic with degrees
text:
Why you cannot do arithmetic with degrees

One degree of latitude ≈ 111 km everywhere
One degree of longitude ≈ 111 km × cos(latitude)

at the equator: 111 km
at 24° (Kruger): ~102 km
at 46° (Switzerland): ~77 km
at the pole: 0 km



# WRONG — mixes two different units
sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2)

Euclidean distance on longitude/latitude is meaningless. You either project to a metric CRS, or compute great-circle distances on the ellipsoid. sf does the second automatically for EPSG:4326 — which is safe, but slower, and does not fix your plots.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
section: One degree is not one distance
text:
One degree is not one distance

Every circle has an 800 km radius on the ground. Plotted as if degrees were metres, they stretch east–west — badly at high latitudes.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
Projected coordinates

Every projection preserves some properties and destroys othersConformal keeps angles/shape (Mercator, UTM). Equal-area keeps area (Albers, Mollweide). Equidistant keeps distances from a point. No projection keeps everything.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
UTM: the practical default

The world is cut into 60 zones, each 6° of longitude wide
Each zone gets its own transverse Mercator projection, so distortion inside a zone is small (< 0.1%)
Coordinates in metres: easting and northing
Kruger is in zone 36S → EPSG:32736
Switzerland is in zone 32N → EPSG:32632



UTM works beautifully inside one zone. Leo the vulture crosses many zones and 47° of latitude, so no single UTM zone fits him. For continental-scale tracks use an equal-area CRS suited to the region — or work in geographic coordinates with geodesic distances.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
section: Choose the projection for the analysis
text:
Choose the projection for the analysis
No projection preserves everything, so pick the property your analysis needs:








You will compute…
Preserve…
Typical choice




Step lengths, distances
distance

angles / shape

A continent-scale migration

Inside one UTM zone the distortions are under 0.1%, so UTM does all three well enough. The choice only becomes real when your animal leaves the zone.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit

The same circles, two projections

Every red disc covers the same 2.5 million km². Web Mercator inflates them towards the poles; an equal-area projection keeps their areas equal, at the cost of their shapes.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
Quiz

You have buffalo fixes in EPSG:4326 and you want the area of a 95% home range polygon, in km². What is the right sequence?

Compute the polygon in 4326, then convert degrees² to km²
Transform the points to EPSG:32736, compute the polygon, read the area in m²
Transform to EPSG:3857, compute the polygon, read the area in m²
Compute the polygon in 4326 — sf handles it automatically


Project first, to a CRS whose units are metres and which is appropriate for the region — UTM 36S for Kruger. Then all the geometry operations are ordinary plane geometry and areas come out in m².
There is no fixed conversion from degrees² to km²: the factor depends on latitude. Web Mercator (3857) has units of metres but is not equal-area, so areas are systematically wrong. And while sf can compute geodesic lengths and areas on 4326, kernel-density home-range estimators need projected coordinates — they assume a plane.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
The idea behind sf
A simple feature data frame is an ordinary data frame with one extra column, geometry, that holds the coordinates — and a CRS attached.

```{r}
library(sf)

pts <- data.frame(
  id = c("a", "b"),
  lon = c(31.76, 31.80),
  lat = c(-24.54, -24.50)
)

pts_sf <- st_as_sf(pts, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)
pts_sf
```

Simple feature collection with 2 features and 3 fields
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 31.76 ymin: -24.54 xmax: 31.8 ymax: -24.5
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
  id   lon    lat             geometry
1  a 31.76 -24.54 POINT (31.76 -24.54)
2  b 31.80 -24.50   POINT (31.8 -24.5)

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
Everything else is dplyr
Because it is a data frame, all your usual verbs work, and the geometry comes along for the ride.

```{r}
library(dplyr)

pts_sf |>
  mutate(label = toupper(id)) |>
  filter(lat > -24.52) |>
  select(id, label)
```

Simple feature collection with 1 feature and 2 fields
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY
Bounding box:  xmin: 31.8 ymin: -24.5 xmax: 31.8 ymax: -24.5
Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84

1  b     B POINT (31.8 -24.5)

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
section: st_crs() vs st_transform() — the classic bug
text:
st_crs() vs st_transform() — the classic bug


st_crs(x) <- 32736
“These numbers were always UTM; I am just writing down the label.”
If the numbers are actually degrees, you have now lied to R. Your buffalo are now in Antarctica (next slide).

st_transform(x, 32736)
“These numbers are in the current CRS; compute the corresponding UTM coordinates.”
The numbers change. This is almost always what you want.



Assign a CRS only when the data arrived without one and you know what it should be. Otherwise, transform.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
Where the mislabelled buffalo went












(31.76, −24.54) read as metres in UTM 36S is a spot 31 m east and 24 m south of the zone’s false origin: 500 km west of the 33°E meridian and 10,000 km south of the equator.
That is (57°W, 85.5°S) — the Antarctic ice sheet. No error, no warning.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
Quiz

Your colleague sends a CSV of coordinates like x = 375051, y = 7285726 and says “they’re from Kruger”. What are they, and what do you do?

Longitude/latitude — use crs = 4326
UTM 36S metres — set crs = 32736 with st_as_sf(), do not transform
Web Mercator — set crs = 3857
Impossible to know


Magnitudes give it away. Longitude and latitude are bounded by ±180 and ±90, so six- and seven-digit values cannot be degrees. Values of that size in metres with a large northing are classic UTM, and Kruger is zone 36S (EPSG:32736) — the 7,285,726 m northing is the southern-hemisphere false northing at ~24.5°S.
Because the numbers are already UTM, you declare the CRS when building the sf object (crs = 32736) rather than transforming. Transforming would treat metres as degrees.
Sanity check afterwards: st_transform(x, 4326) and confirm you land at roughly 31.8°E, 24.5°S.

r <- rast(nrows = 4, ncols = 6,
          xmin = 31.5, xmax = 32.1, ymin = -24.8, ymax = -24.4,
          crs = "EPSG:4326")
values(r) <- 1:ncell(r)

text:
What defines a raster

Extent — xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax
Resolution — cell size in CRS units. res(r)
Dimensions — rows × columns × layers. dim(r)
CRS — same concept as for vectors
Values — one per cell per layer, possibly NA


A multi-layer raster (SpatRaster with several layers) is how you store a time series: one NDVI layer per 16-day composite, stacked. That is exactly what we need in Session 3.

section: The terra functions you will use
text:
The terra functions you will use



Function
What it does

create or read a raster

extract() is the bridge between the movement world and the environment world. Almost everything from Session 3 onwards passes through it.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
Rasters and vectors must agree
Before extract(), three things must line up:

Same CRS. If both objects carry a CRS, terra transforms for you and warns. If either lacks one — a bare coordinate matrix — it assumes they match.
Overlapping extents. Non-overlap gives you a column of NA, not an error.
Appropriate resolution. Extracting a 1 km NDVI cell for a fix with 10 m GPS error is fine. Extracting a 10 m Sentinel pixel for an Argos fix with 5 km error is self-deception.



Match the resolution of your environmental data to the error of your locations. A pixel finer than your positional error adds noise, not information.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
Quiz

You run terra::extract(ndvi, cbind(buffalo$lon, buffalo$lat)) and every value comes back NA. The NDVI raster is in UTM 36S. What happened?

A bare coordinate matrix carries no CRS, so terra assumed the degrees were already metres
terra always errors on a CRS mismatch, so this cannot happen
The NDVI raster is empty
You must call crop() before extract()


Modern terra is helpful when it can be: give it a SpatVector or an sf object that carries a CRS, and it transforms your points for you, printing a warning:
[extract] transforming vector data to the CRS of the raster
But a plain two-column matrix has no CRS. terra can only assume the numbers are already in the raster’s coordinate system — so 31.8 and −24.5 are read as metres, land far outside the extent, and every lookup returns NA.
The same silent failure happens if the CRS of either object is missing (crs(r) <- ""). Lesson: keep your data in objects that carry their CRS, and never strip coordinates down to a bare matrix just to pass them along.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
section: Why vegetation looks the way it does
text:
Why vegetation looks the way it does


Healthy green vegetation:

absorbs strongly in the red (~660 nm) — chlorophyll is doing photosynthesis
reflects strongly in the near infrared (~850 nm) — the internal leaf structure scatters it

So the contrast between red and NIR is a measure of green biomass.


That single fact is the basis of essentially every vegetation index ever published.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
Spectral signatures

Schematic curves. Vegetation is dark in the red and bright in the near infrared; soil and water are not. NDVI measures exactly that contrast.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
NDVI
\[\text{NDVI} = \frac{\text{NIR} - \text{Red}}{\text{NIR} + \text{Red}}\]

Ranges −1 to +1. Water < 0; bare soil/rock ~0.1–0.2; sparse vegetation ~0.2–0.4; dense green vegetation 0.6–0.9
A proxy for green biomass and primary productivity
Normalised, so it partly cancels illumination and viewing-angle effects








It saturates. Above ~0.8 — closed canopy — NDVI stops responding to extra biomass. In rainforest it is nearly flat and nearly useless.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
Kruger, wet and dry

MODIS NDVI at 250 m, the same landscape six months apart (dots: Cilla’s fixes). An NDVI value is only meaningful together with its date.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
You cannot have all four

Spatial — pixel size. 10 m (Sentinel-2) … 500 m (MODIS) … 25 km (some climate products)
Temporal — revisit time. 5 days (Sentinel-2) vs daily (MODIS) vs 16 days (Landsat)
Spectral — number and width of bands. 4 broad bands vs 200 narrow (hyperspectral)
Radiometric — bit depth; how finely brightness is quantised



They trade off against each other: a detector collecting light from a small patch, in a narrow band, gets few photons — so it needs a longer dwell time, which means a narrower swath and a longer revisit.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
Pixel size changes the landscape

The same February NDVI around Cilla’s range at MODIS resolution, then averaged to ~1 km and ~5 km. At 5 km every fix gets nearly the same value.

title: Spatial data in R: the survival kit
text:
Quiz

You study habitat selection by a forest ungulate using GPS collars (error ~15 m, hourly fixes) in a landscape with small forest patches of 1–5 ha. Which product for vegetation cover?

MODIS NDVI, 250 m, daily
Sentinel-2, 10–20 m, every 5 days
A 1 km global land-cover map
Sentinel-1 SAR, 10 m


A 1–5 ha patch is roughly 100–220 m across. A 250 m MODIS pixel is larger than the patch, so every fix would get a mixed value averaging forest and open land — the very contrast you are trying to measure would be erased. A 1 km product is hopeless for the same reason.
Sentinel-2 at 10–20 m resolves those patches comfortably, and its 5-day revisit captures the growing season. Its resolution is also well matched to 15 m GPS error: finer would just add noise.
Sentinel-1 is excellent for structure and for cloudy regions, but it does not measure greenness — it is the right answer to a different question.

title: From fixes to trajectories
section: What a GPS track actually is
text:
What a GPS track actually is

A set of point estimates, each with an error, at irregular moments
Between two fixes the animal went somewhere; the straight line is an assumption, not an observation
Interpolating a position between fixes invents data — useful for plotting, dangerous for inference
Every derived quantity — step length, speed, turning angle — inherits both the sampling interval and the location error



A track is a sample of a continuous path. Treat every line you draw between fixes as a hypothesis.

title: From fixes to trajectories
text:
The step
Two consecutive fixes define a step.



Step length \(s_t = \lVert \mathbf{x}_{t+1} - \mathbf{x}_t \rVert\)
Absolute direction \(\phi_t = \operatorname{atan2}(\Delta y, \Delta x)\)
Turning angle \(\theta_t = \phi_t - \phi_{t-1}\), wrapped to \((-\pi, \pi]\)
Speed \(v_t = s_t / \Delta t\)



A turning angle needs three fixes. A step needs two. That is why filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3) exists.



Turning angles are circular data: −179° and +179° are 2° apart, not 358°. Never take an arithmetic mean of angles.

Steps and turns of a real buffalo

Cilla, hourly steps. Short steps dominate; turning angles concentrate near 0° (keep going). The bars at −180° and +180° are the same reversal, split in two by the axis.

title: From fixes to trajectories
section: Location error: why you cannot connect the dots
text:
Location error: why you cannot connect the dots

A 15 m error on each fix is negligible on a 1 km step, and dominates a 20 m step
For short steps the direction is mostly noise, so turning angles look random exactly when the animal is resting
A single bad fix creates a spike: an impossible step out and back
Error is not independent white noise: it is correlated in time and worse in closed habitat



Resting animals look like they are wandering at random, and spikes look like sprints. Neither is behaviour. Both reach your models unless you look first.

From fixes to trajectories
section: The four things that are always wrong
text:
The four things that are always wrong

Duplicated fixes — same individual, same timestamp. The collar re-transmitted. ~13% of our buffalo file.
Missing coordinates — a row exists, the location failed.
Impossible locations — (0, 0), land animals at sea, points on another continent. Usually a corrupt transmission.
Speed outliers — a fix that implies 200 km/h for a buffalo, then a return. A spike.



Clean in this order, and count what you remove at each step. A cleaning step that silently deletes 30% of your data has changed your study.

title: From fixes to trajectories
section: Duplicates are not all the same
text:
Duplicates are not all the same

Exact duplicates — every field identical. Safe to drop.
Same timestamp, different coordinates — which is right? Keep the one with better quality (more satellites, lower DOP); if you cannot tell, keep the first and document it.
Near-duplicates — timestamps a few seconds apart. These create near-zero dt and therefore enormous apparent speeds.


# Blunt but explicit
trk |> distinct(id, t_, .keep_all = TRUE)

# move2 is more careful about the ambiguous case
move2::mt_filter_unique(x, criterion = "first")

title: From fixes to trajectories
text:
Speed filtering: useful and dangerous

Compute speed between consecutive fixes; drop anything above a biologically plausible maximum
Buffalo ~ 10 km/h sustained; vulture ~ 80 km/h in flight
The danger: a threshold that is too low deletes real fast movement — exactly the migration or escape events you may care about
The subtlety: one bad fix creates two fast steps (out and back). Naïve filters often delete the good neighbour instead of the bad point



Never filter silently. Plot what you are about to remove, look at it, then remove it. The sdafilter/argosfilter approach — which tests whether a point is fast and forms a spike — is better than a plain speed threshold.

title: From fixes to trajectories
text:
Quiz

You remove all fixes implying a speed above 15 km/h from the buffalo data, and your dataset shrinks by 0.4%. Then you compute mean daily displacement and it drops by 18%. What is the most likely explanation?

The filter worked correctly; the old value was inflated by errors
Many removed “fast” steps were actually short time gaps, not long distances
Buffalo never exceed 15 km/h so nothing real was removed
Daily displacement is unrelated to speed


Speed is distance divided by time. A pair of fixes 40 seconds apart — a near-duplicate — gives a huge apparent speed even if the animal moved 200 m. Filtering on speed therefore preferentially removes fixes with small time gaps, not fixes with large distances.
An 18% change in a summary statistic from deleting 0.4% of rows is a red flag that the filter is doing something other than what you intended.
Correct order: remove duplicates and near-duplicates first, resample to a regular interval second, and only then consider a speed filter — on steps that share a common dt.

HMMs (Session 8) assume a regular interval; irregular data need a continuous-time model instead
SSFs (Session 7) compare each observed step to alternatives of the same duration
KDE home ranges assume roughly even coverage in time

Two ways to hold a trajectory


adehabitatLT::ltraj
The classic (Calenge 2006). One data frame per burst, with dist, dt, R2n (squared displacement), abs.angle and rel.angle precomputed.
redisltraj() regularises by interpolating new positions.

A tidy tibble. Steps, angles and covariates are computed when you ask.
track_resample() regularises by selecting existing fixes.



The two “regularise” functions do opposite things. One keeps only what you observed; the other manufactures positions you did not observe.

title: From fixes to trajectories

Selecting versus interpolating

Toni across a 9-hour gap. Selection ends the burst at the gap; interpolation fills it with evenly spaced positions on a straight line the buffalo almost certainly did not walk.

title: From fixes to trajectories
section: Truncation: the start and the end
text:
Truncation: the start and the end

After capture — animals often behave abnormally for days (flight, restricted movement). Many studies discard a fixed post-capture window
Before the end — a collar that stops moving may mean a dead animal or a dropped collar, not a resting one
At gaps — a burst ends wherever fixes are missing; steps are never computed across a gap



Decide the truncation rules before you look at the results, write them down, and report how much data they removed.

text:
Resampling and bursts
track_resample() keeps fixes that fall on a regular grid within a tolerance, and labels contiguous runs as bursts.
trk |>
  track_resample(rate = hours(1), tolerance = minutes(10)) |>
  filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3)

rate — the interval you want
tolerance — how much slack. Too tight and you throw away good data; too loose and “hourly” steps are really 40–80 minutes
A burst breaks wherever a fix is missing. Steps are computed within bursts, never across a gap
min_n = 3 because a turning angle needs three points

title: From fixes to trajectories
text:
Quiz

track_resample() interpolates missing locations to give you a regular series. True or false?

True — that is what resampling means
False — it selects existing fixes and discards the rest


amt::track_resample() is a filter, not an interpolator. It walks the track and keeps the fixes that fall close enough to a regular time grid; where no fix is available, the burst simply ends. You never gain observations you did not make.
That is deliberate. Interpolating locations invents data and then feeds the invention into a model as if it were an observation, which biases step-length and turning-angle distributions towards straighter, slower movement.
If you genuinely need locations between fixes, use a model that says so — a continuous-time movement model (ctmm) or a state-space model — which gives you interpolated positions with uncertainty attached.

title: From fixes to trajectories
text:
Quiz

A colleague reports a mean sampling interval of 2.45 hours for a collar programmed to fix hourly. What does that number actually tell you?

The collar was reprogrammed partway through
Almost nothing about the schedule — a few very long gaps have inflated the mean
The fix success rate was about 41%
The animal was inactive, so the collar skipped fixes


The median for this collar is 1 hour — the schedule is intact. The mean is 2.45 h because the distribution has a long tail: one gap of 2,523 hours (105 days) drags it up on its own.
A mean sampling interval is a summary of your collar failures, not of your sampling design. Report the median, the maximum gap, and the number of gaps beyond some threshold.
And no, you cannot read the fix success rate off the mean. Success rate is the proportion of scheduled attempts that returned a location, which you get by dividing each gap by the modal interval and counting the misses.

title: From fixes to trajectories
text:
The operation
For every fix, look up the environment there and then.

Static covariates — elevation, slope, distance to river. One raster; extract() and done.
Dynamic covariates — NDVI, temperature, snow. A stack of rasters with timestamps. You must match each fix to the right layer.



A track that spans two years annotated with a single NDVI image is not annotated — it is decorated. If your covariate varies in time and your analysis does not, you have thrown away the mechanism.

title: From fixes to trajectories
text:
Decorated versus annotated

Queen in 2005. One February image says she lived in green vegetation all year. Matched in time, NDVI halves by September — and the months with no composite nearby are honestly blank.

Doing it in time
# Which layer does each fix belong to?
layer_dates <- as.Date(c("2005-01-01", "2005-01-17", ...))

idx <- findInterval(as.Date(trk$t_), layer_dates)

# Extract from the whole stack, then pick the right column per row
vals <- terra::extract(ndvi_stack, vect(trk))[, -1]
trk$ndvi <- vals[cbind(seq_len(nrow(vals)), idx)]

Movebank Env-DATA does this for you, including interpolation in time, for dozens of products. Use it for real projects — but understand what it is doing first, which is what today’s exercise is for.

title: From fixes to trajectories
text:
Quiz

You annotate two years of buffalo fixes with a single dry-season NDVI image and find a strong positive selection for high NDVI. What is the main problem?

NDVI saturates in dense vegetation
The covariate is static while both the animal and the vegetation varied seasonally
The pixel size is too coarse
NDVI cannot be used for savanna


The image describes one moment. Over two years, vegetation in a savanna swings enormously between wet and dry season, and the buffalo’s needs swing with it. By holding NDVI fixed you have conflated “places that were green in that dry season” with “places that are green when the animal was there”.
What you have measured is selection for persistently productive places — which may be interesting, but is not what the model claims.
The result can even be the opposite sign from the time-matched analysis: an animal may select the greenest available patch at every moment while showing no preference for places that are green on average.
Fix: use a time series and match each fix to the contemporaneous layer.
