title: Quantifying movement
text:
Today

Internal state Motion capacity Navigation capacity External factors Movement path

From numbers describing a path to inferences about behaviour — the first time we try to climb from the bottom box to the ones above it.

title: Quantifying movement
text:
Where we are going


Path-level descriptors: net squared displacement, straightness, sinuosity, fractal dimension
Classifying movement strategies from NSD curves (Bunnefeld et al. 2011)
First-passage time and the scale of area-restricted search
Behavioural modes along a path: encamped versus transit
Simple segmentation: thresholds, expert rules, behavioural change-point analysis




Every method today returns a confident-looking answer. The skill is asking whether it describes the animal or the sampling.

title: Quantifying movement
text:
Everything here is scale-dependent

Sample every 5 minutes: many short steps — but so short that GPS error randomises their direction
Sample hourly: clear directional persistence
Sample every 12 hours: few long steps, turning angles ≈ uniform (the animal looks like it moves at random)
Total path length grows without bound as the interval shrinks — the coastline paradox



“Mean step length” is not a property of the animal. It is a property of the animal and your sampling interval. Always report the interval alongside it, and never compare step lengths measured at different rates.
There is a sweet spot: fine enough to resolve the behaviour, coarse enough that a typical step is much longer than your GPS error.

title: Quantifying movement
section: The coastline paradox, in a buffalo
text:
The coastline paradox, in a buffalo

The same buffalo, Cilla, resampled to coarser and coarser intervals. Neither number is a property of the animal alone.

title: Quantifying movement
text:
Straightness and sinuosity


Straightness index
\[\text{ST} = \frac{D}{L}\] Net displacement over path length, between 0 and 1.
Intuitive, but it depends on the length of the window you compute it over.

Sinuosity (Benhamou 2004)
Built from the step length and the concentration of turning angles.
Describes the local tortuosity of a random search path, and is far less sensitive to the window.



Use straightness for oriented movement (how directly did it get there?) and sinuosity for searching movement (how much does it wiggle?).

title: Quantifying movement
text:
Fractal dimension

Measure path length with a “ruler” of length \(r\); on a fractal path \(L(r) \propto r^{1-D}\), so \(D\) comes from the slope of log L on log r
\(D = 1\): straight line; \(D \to 2\): a path that fills the plane
Appealing because it claims to be scale-free
The catch (Benhamou 2004; Turchin 1996): real animal paths are rarely fractal across more than a narrow range of scales, and \(D\) estimated from a correlated random walk varies with \(r\)



If \(D\) changes with the ruler, the path is not fractal — and the change itself tells you the scale at which the behaviour changes.

title: Quantifying movement
text:
Net squared displacement (NSD)
\[\text{NSD}(t) = \lVert \mathbf{x}_t - \mathbf{x}_0 \rVert^2\]
The squared distance from the starting point. A remarkably effective diagnostic:

Sedentary — NSD rises then plateaus at a low value
Migratory — a sigmoid up, a plateau, a sigmoid back down
Dispersal — a single step up to a new plateau
Nomadic — rises roughly linearly, no plateau


Fitting these shapes as competing non-linear models (Bunnefeld et al. 2011) is a cheap and surprisingly effective way to classify movement strategies.

title: Quantifying movement
text:
Four shapes

NSD against time for the four strategies of Bunnefeld et al. (2011).

title: Quantifying movement
text:
Classifying strategies from NSD
Bunnefeld et al. (2011) fit competing non-linear models to each NSD curve and let the data choose:








Strategy
NSD shape
Model




Nomad
keeps rising
\(\beta t\)


Resident
rises, then plateaus
\(c\,(1 - e^{-kt})\)


Disperser
one sigmoid step
\(\delta / (1 + e^{(\theta - t)/\phi})\)


Migrant
up, plateau, back down
difference of two sigmoids





The fitted parameters are the biology: \(\sqrt{\delta}\) is the migration distance, \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) the departure and return dates. Never report the winning model without looking at them.

title: Quantifying movement
text:
A real migrant: Leo

Daily NSD of the vulture Leo, June 2007 to May 2008, and the fitted migrant model. The parameters read as biology: a migration distance in thousands of kilometres, a departure date and a return date.

title: Quantifying movement
text:
Quiz

You fit the four NSD models to a year of data for a savanna buffalo, and the migrant model wins by ΔAIC = 60. The fitted displacement is 12 km. What do you conclude?

The buffalo is a migrant
It shifted within its range; AIC picked the most flexible curve, and the parameters say it is not a migration
The resident model must have failed to converge
Buffalo cannot be classified with NSD


The double-sigmoid “migrant” curve is the most flexible of the four: it also fits an animal that drifts to one side of its home range for a few months and comes back. AIC rewards that fit — and with hundreds of autocorrelated daily points, AIC differences are grossly inflated.
The parameters settle it: 12 km is a home-range-scale shift. A real migrant such as Leo the vulture gives a displacement of thousands of kilometres. Read the parameters, not just the winner.

title: Quantifying movement
text:
Quiz

Two studies report mean step length for the same population of roe deer. Study A reports 180 m, study B reports 640 m. Both are competent. What is the most likely explanation?

Study B’s collars had worse GPS accuracy
Study B sampled at a longer interval
Study B included migratory individuals
One of them made an arithmetic error


Step length scales with the sampling interval. An animal sampled hourly produces shorter steps than the same animal sampled every four hours, because the straight line between fixes cuts across all the wiggles in between.
This is why step length is not comparable across studies unless the interval matches, and why you must state the interval in every methods section.
It is also why Session 7’s step selection functions always compare an observed step with alternatives of exactly the same duration.

title: Quantifying movement
section: How long to leave a circle?
text:
How long to leave a circle?
Fauchald & Tveraa (2003): around each fix, draw a circle of radius \(r\) and measure the time the animal takes to leave it.

Where the animal searches intensively, first-passage time (FPT) is long; where it travels, FPT is short
Repeat for many radii and compute the variance of log FPT along the path
The radius at which that variance peaks is the spatial scale of area-restricted search



FPT turns “where does the animal slow down?” into a scale: how big are the patches it responds to?

title: Quantifying movement
text:
First-passage time, drawn

A simulated animal alternating travel and intensive search. Inside a patch it takes many hours to leave a 400 m circle; in transit, one or two.

title: Quantifying movement
text:
Quiz

You compute var(log FPT) for radii from 25 m to 8 km for an hourly buffalo track. It is highest at 25 m, falls to a minimum at 1.5 km, then rises to a second peak near 4 km. Which peak is the scale of area-restricted search?

25 m — it is the highest
~4 km — the small-radius values are inflated by resting and GPS error
1.5 km — the minimum
Neither; FPT only works for seabirds


At radii comparable to GPS error and to the distance a resting animal shuffles, FPT is dominated by noise and by long bouts of doing nothing: its variance is high for reasons that have nothing to do with searching.
The meaningful signal is the peak at a scale well above the positional error — here about 4 km, the scale at which this buffalo concentrates its use. Always interpret FPT only for radii several times larger than your location error and typical resting movement.

title: Quantifying movement
text:
The problem
An animal is not doing one thing all day.

Resting, foraging, travelling, migrating — each with its own step-length and turning-angle signature
Pool them and every summary is a meaningless average: a “mean step length” that describes no actual behaviour
Leo’s six-year track contains residency and migration. A single home range spans two continents (Session 1)



Segment first, then analyse. Almost every method in this course assumes a homogeneous process. Segmentation is how you earn that assumption.

title: Quantifying movement
text:
Encamped versus transit
The simplest useful classification has two modes:


Encamped
Short steps, frequent reversals, low net displacement.
Resting, ruminating, foraging within a patch.

Transit
Long steps, turning angles near zero, high net displacement.
Travelling between patches, to water, away from danger.


Finer schemes — resting / foraging / travelling — need either finer sampling or extra sensors (accelerometers). With hourly GPS, two or three modes is usually all the data can resolve.

title: Quantifying movement
text:
Two questions, often confused


Change-point detection
“Where does the process change?”
Finds breakpoints in a time series. Output: a set of segments.
BCPA, segclust2d, penalised contrasts.

State classification
“Which of \(N\) recurring states is the animal in now?”
Assigns every step to a state, and states can recur.
HMM, EMbC, state-space models.


“Migration started on 14 September” is a change-point question. “Was this step foraging or travelling?” is a state question. Choose the tool that matches the question.

title: Quantifying movement
text:
The families








Approach
Idea
Notes




Thresholding
“Speed > 2 m/s = travelling”
Transparent; arbitrary; no uncertainty


First-passage time
Time to leave a circle of radius r
Good for finding scales of area-restricted search


BCPA
Change points in persistence velocity
Behavioural Change Point Analysis; needs a tuning choice


Clustering / EMbC
Cluster steps in (speed, turn) space
No time dependence — ignores that behaviour persists


HMM
Latent state chain + state-specific distributions
The standard. Uses time dependence


State-space models
HMM + explicit observation error
Handles messy data; slower, harder

title: Quantifying movement
text:
Thresholds and expert rules

Speed threshold — “steps faster than \(v^*\) are travelling”. Transparent and reproducible
Expert rules — combine several: speed and turning angle and time of day, chosen from knowledge of the species
Both are defensible only when the metric is clearly bimodal — a histogram with an empty valley between modes
Without that valley, the threshold is an arbitrary decision dressed up as a result

title: Quantifying movement
section: An honest threshold, and a dishonest one
text:
An honest threshold, and a dishonest one

Left: Leo’s migration days (> 50 km, dashed) form a separate mode. Right: the buffalo’s speeds are a continuum with no gap; any cut-off is arbitrary.

title: Quantifying movement
text:
Behavioural change-point analysis
BCPA (Gurarie et al. 2009) looks for places where the statistical properties of the movement change.

Works on a single variable, typically persistence velocity \(V\cos\theta\): fast and straight gives high values
Slides a window along the track; within each window finds the most likely break in mean, variance or autocorrelation
Collects breaks that recur across windows into change points
Works with irregular sampling, which is its great practical strength



BCPA tells you where the process changes. It does not tell you what the animal was doing, and it cannot know whether a change is behavioural or a change in your collar’s schedule.

BCPA on Cilla

title: Quantifying movement
text:
Quiz

BCPA on 25 days of hourly buffalo data, window of 50 fixes: 29 phases. Window of 30 fixes: 38. Same 50-fix window on the track resampled to 3-hourly: 19. How many behavioural phases did the buffalo go through?

29 — the default settings
19 — hourly data are too noisy
38 — more resolution finds more behaviour
The question has no single answer: phase counts depend on window size and fix rate


These are real results for the buffalo Cilla. The window size is an analyst’s tuning choice, and the fix rate sets what a “window of 50 fixes” means in time: 50 hours at hourly sampling, 150 hours at 3-hourly. Match the window in duration (17 fixes at 3-hourly ≈ 50 hours) and the 3-hourly count rises back to 29.
A phase count is a property of the analysis, not of the animal. What you can interpret biologically are the change points that persist across reasonable windows and fix rates — which is the robustness check you run in today’s practical.

Today

Random walks are the simplest possible answers to how an animal moves and where it is heading. Their value is not realism — it is that they tell you what to expect if nothing else were going on.

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
Where we are going


Why simulate: you cannot rewind an animal, but you can simulate a null
The uncorrelated random walk and mean squared displacement
Correlated random walks: persistence, and the scales of movement
Biased random walks: advection versus diffusion
Lévy walks — and an honest account of the controversy
Using simulations as hypothesis tests




Today’s practical builds a simulator from scratch. The same simulated animal becomes the ground truth you test estimators against in Sessions 6 and 7.

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
You cannot rewind an animal

A tracking study observes one realisation of a random process
To ask “is this unusual?” you need the distribution of what could have happened — and nature will not rerun the experiment
A movement model is a recipe that generates tracks. Run it a thousand times and you have that distribution
Compare the real track with the simulated ones: where does it fall?



A random walk is a null model. When the animal departs from it, the departure is the biology: memory, attraction, avoidance, a home range.

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
Four canonical walks

Same number of steps. Red triangle: start. Cross: the goal of the biased walk.

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
The Brownian baseline

Each step has a random length and a uniformly random direction, independent of the previous one
The animal has no memory and no goal
After \(n\) steps the expected squared distance from the start — the mean squared displacement — is \[\text{MSD}(n) = n\,\mathrm{E}[l^2]\]
MSD grows linearly with time: \(\text{MSD} = 4Dt\) in two dimensions, with \(D\) the diffusion coefficient



Linear MSD means the typical distance from the start grows only as \(\sqrt{t}\). A random walker four times as long gets only twice as far.

title: Movement models and simulation
Movement models and simulation
text:
Persistence
A correlated random walk (CRW) draws each new heading close to the last:
\[\phi_t = \phi_{t-1} + \theta_t, \qquad \theta_t \sim \text{von Mises}(0, \kappa)\]

\(\kappa = 0\): turning angles uniform — the uncorrelated walk
large \(\kappa\): turning angles near zero — nearly straight lines
Step lengths from a gamma, Weibull or log-normal distribution
Two parameters for steps, one for turns: the same ingredients as the step selection functions of Session 7 and the hidden Markov models of Session 8

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
The two ingredients

Every random walk in this session, and every SSF and HMM later, is built from one distribution of each kind.

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
The scales of movement

Short lags: persistence makes a CRW ballistic (MSD ∝ t²). Long lags: it forgets its direction and becomes diffusive (MSD ∝ t). The crossover is the scale of the animal’s directional memory.

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
Quiz

You plot MSD against lag on log–log axes for a real track. The slope is ~1.8 at lags up to 3 hours, then ~1.0 up to 10 days, then flattens to ~0. What does each regime suggest?

Nothing — MSD is always linear for real animals
Directed movement at short scales, random-walk-like at intermediate scales, and confinement to a home range at long scales
GPS error at short scales, directed movement at long scales
The track needs resampling


Slope near 2: ballistic, persistent movement — the animal keeps its heading for a few hours. Slope near 1: diffusive, a correlated random walk has forgotten its direction. Slope near 0: MSD stops growing because the animal cannot get any further from where it was — a home range.
That last regime is what an unbiased random walk can never produce, and it is the starting point of Session 6. One caution: very short lags can also look flat because GPS error sets a floor on the smallest measurable displacement.

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
Advection and diffusion
Add a preferred direction — towards a den, a water hole, a breeding ground:

Biased random walk (BRW): each heading drawn around the bearing to the goal, with no memory of the last heading
Biased correlated random walk (BCRW): a compromise between the previous heading (persistence) and the bearing to the goal (bias)
Two processes act at once: advection (drift towards the goal, distance ∝ \(t\)) and diffusion (random spread, distance ∝ \(\sqrt{t}\))
Over long enough times, advection always wins



Weak bias is invisible over a few steps and decisive over many. That is why orientation mechanisms are so hard to detect in short tracks and so obvious in migrations.

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
Drift beats spread, eventually

A weak pull towards the east (bias weight 0.1). For the first 170 steps the random spread is larger than the progress; after that, drift wins for good.

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
Central places
A BCRW whose goal is its own home produces something new: the animal wanders, drifts back, wanders again. It never escapes.

The track stays within a bounded area: a home range emerges from a simple movement rule
The long-run spread of positions is a stationary utilisation distribution
Mechanistic home-range models (Moorcroft & Lewis 2006) build on exactly this idea



In the practical this central-place walker becomes our ground-truth animal: we know its true home range, so in Session 6 we can check which estimator gets it right.

title: Movement models and simulation
section: A home range from one rule
text:
A home range from one rule

No memory, no map, no boundary — only a weak pull towards home. Dashed: the true 95% range, about 800 km², which Session 6 tries to recover.

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
Quiz

A homing pigeon is simulated as a BCRW with a weak bias towards its loft. Over the first 10 steps its track is indistinguishable from an unbiased CRW. Over 500 steps it heads unmistakably home. Why?

The bias strength increases with time
Drift accumulates linearly with time while random spread grows only with its square root
The CRW component weakens over time
Simulation error


The bias adds a small, consistent component to every step: after \(n\) steps the drift has accumulated in proportion to \(n\). The random component partly cancels itself out, growing only as \(\sqrt{n}\). Eventually the drift must dominate.
Detecting orientation in real animals is hard for exactly this reason: over a short track, even a genuine bias is swamped by noise.

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
The Lévy hypothesis

Step lengths drawn from a power law: \(P(l) \propto l^{-\mu}\), with \(1 < \mu \le 3\)
No characteristic scale: many short steps, occasional enormous ones
Viswanathan et al. (1996) reported Lévy flights in wandering albatrosses; Viswanathan et al. (1999) showed that \(\mu \approx 2\) is an optimal search strategy for sparse, randomly placed targets
A seductive idea: a universal, scale-free rule for foraging

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
The reversal

Edwards et al. (2007) reanalysed the albatross data with better records: the long “flights” included time sitting on the water. The Lévy pattern disappeared
They also showed that log–log regression of histograms, the standard method at the time, is biased; power laws must be fitted by maximum likelihood and compared with alternatives (Clauset et al. 2009)
Benhamou (2007): an animal switching between two behaviours, each a simple random walk, produces a step-length distribution that a power law fits beautifully
Lévy-like patterns do appear in some marine predators, but depend on environmental context (Sims et al. 2008; Humphries et al. 2010)



The honest position: a power-law fit is not evidence of a Lévy strategy. Different mechanisms produce indistinguishable step-length distributions.

title: Movement models and simulation
section: Two ways to make a heavy tail
text:
Two ways to make a heavy tail

Grey: one exponential. Gold: a true power law. Red: two exponential modes, no power law anywhere — yet heavy-tailed enough that a power law beats a single exponential by thousands of AIC units.

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
Quiz

You fit an exponential and a power law to 2,000 step lengths by maximum likelihood. The power law wins by more than 2,000 AIC units. What have you shown?

The animal performs a Lévy walk
The animal optimises its search
The step lengths are heavy-tailed — which a mixture of two behaviours can produce just as well
The exponential model failed to converge


In the practical you will generate exactly this result from a mixture of two exponential distributions — a short-step mode and a long-step mode, and no power law anywhere. The power law wins decisively anyway.
A fit tells you about the shape of a distribution. It cannot tell you which process generated it. To argue for a Lévy strategy you would need to rule out composite walks — for instance by showing that the long steps do not belong to a distinct behavioural state (Session 8).

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
The recipe

Choose a statistic that captures your question — net displacement, radius of gyration, time to reach water
Choose a null process that lacks the mechanism you are testing — a CRW with the animal’s own step and turn distributions, but no memory
Simulate it many times; compute the statistic each time
Locate the observed value in the simulated distribution



The null must match the animal in everything except the mechanism. A null with the wrong step lengths is a straw man, and rejecting it proves nothing.

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
The recipe, applied

Grey-green: 300 CRWs with the buffalo’s own steps and turns. Red line: the buffalo. Only the longer track is clearly more confined than its null.

title: Movement models and simulation
text:
Quiz

You test whether a buffalo is range-resident by comparing its radius of gyration with 300 CRWs built from its own steps and turns. For a 36-day track it sits at the 73rd percentile; for a 157-day track of another buffalo, the 1st. What is the most important lesson?

Only the second buffalo is range-resident
The test is broken
Confinement is detectable only when the track is much longer than the time needed to cross the range
More simulations would make the first test significant


These are real results for the Kruger buffalo. Over a month, a resident and a random walker cover similar ground: the resident has not yet had time to hit the edges of its range. Only over months does the random walker keep spreading while the resident stays put.
More simulations only sharpen the null distribution; they do not add information about the animal. This is the tracking duration versus occupation timescale problem — and exactly what the variogram in Session 6 diagnoses.

A home range is what a path looks like when memory (navigation) and the distribution of resources (external factors) keep an animal in one place. Today: how to estimate it — and when it does not exist.

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
Where we are going


From territorial polygons to probabilistic utilisation distributions
MCP, and why it is still reported
Kernel density estimation, and its sensitivity to bandwidth
Autocorrelation: from nuisance (Brownian bridges) to information (AKDE)
When a home range is a valid concept: stationarity and the occupation timescale




Today’s real learning objective is the comparison: four estimators, one animal, four different answers — and a simulated animal whose true answer we know.

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
Burt’s definition

“That area traversed by the individual in its normal activities of food gathering, mating and caring for young.” — Burt (1943)



Note what it excludes: exploratory forays, migration, dispersal
Note what it does not say: nothing about probability, nothing about 95%
Powell & Mitchell (2012): a home range is the part of its cognitive map an animal chooses to keep up to date — our estimators are crude proxies

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
From polygons to distributions

The same buffalo, Cilla. On the left every part of the area counts the same; on the right, core areas and rarely used edges are distinguished.


The UD is the object; “the home range” is a contour you draw on it. Say which contour, and which estimator produced the UD.

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
MCP
The smallest convex polygon containing \(x\)% of the fixes.


For

Trivial to compute and explain
Comparable with a century of literature
No smoothing parameter to argue about


Against

Convex — includes land never used
Sensitive to outliers and sample size
Area depends on how long you tracked
No density information



Report it for comparability with old studies. Never as your only estimate.

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
MCP on a real buffalo

Left: the 95% MCP (solid) and 100% MCP (dashed) contain large stretches the animal hardly used. Right: the same estimate from the first 5, 10, 15… days.

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
KDE
Put a small bump (kernel) on each fix and sum them into a utilisation distribution (Worton 1989).

Gives a density: core areas, disjoint patches, used and unused parts
The answer is dominated by the bandwidth \(h\)

\(h_\text{ref}\) — optimal if the UD were a single bivariate normal; usually over-smooths real, multi-modal ranges
\(h_\text{LSCV}\) — least-squares cross-validation; often under-smooths into fragments, and frequently fails to converge

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
How a kernel works

Ten fixes (ticks) in one dimension. Each gets a bump (thin lines); their sum (thick line) is the estimated UD. Same fixes, two bandwidths, two stories.

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
Same buffalo, two bandwidths
The buffalo Cilla, hourly fixes over 5 months, 95% contours:



A factor of three from one analyst’s choice. Report the bandwidth selector — and check whether LSCV actually converged. adehabitatHR warns you; papers rarely do.

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
Quiz

You compute a 95% KDE with LSCV and get a range three times smaller than with \(h_\text{ref}\), made of dozens of small islands. kernelUD() printed “the algorithm did not converge”. What do you report?

The LSCV result — it is data-driven and \(h_\text{ref}\) is known to over-smooth
The average of the two
That the KDE area is not well determined by these data, and prefer an estimator that accounts for autocorrelation
The \(h_\text{ref}\) result, because it converged


LSCV fails in a characteristic way on GPS data: with many autocorrelated fixes it chooses a tiny bandwidth that treats every cluster of consecutive fixes as a separate hotspot. A non-converged bandwidth is not a result.
\(h_\text{ref}\) “converges” only because it is a formula — it assumes a unimodal range and has no way to be wrong in public. Neither is trustworthy here. The disagreement itself is the finding: these data do not pin down a KDE area, which points to the autocorrelation-aware methods on the next slides.

title: Home ranges and space use
section: The problem classical KDE has with GPS
text:
The problem classical KDE has with GPS
Classical KDE assumes fixes are independent draws from the UD.

Hourly GPS fixes are nothing of the sort — the animal was 300 m away an hour ago and will be 300 m away in an hour.

The effective sample size is far smaller than \(n\)
The UD comes out too narrow — the range is under-estimated
Collecting more fixes at a higher rate makes it worse, not better




This is why area estimates from 1990s VHF studies (a few dozen fixes, days apart) and modern GPS studies (thousands, an hour apart) are not comparable.

title: Home ranges and space use
section: Same number of fixes, different information
text:
Same number of fixes, different information

The central-place animal from Session 5, whose true range (dashed) we know. Two weeks of dense fixes describe two weeks of the animal, not its range.

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
Brownian bridges: use the path
Horne et al. (2007): between two consecutive fixes the animal was somewhere on a random bridge connecting them.

The uncertainty of the bridge grows with the time gap and shrinks near each fix, scaled by a mobility parameter estimated from the data
Uses the order of the fixes, not just their positions
Handles irregular sampling naturally
Answers a specific question: where was the animal during the tracking period? — its occurrence distribution



A Brownian bridge maps where the animal went, not where it could go. It shrinks around the observed path, so it is usually the smallest of the estimates — correctly so, for the question it answers.

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
Autocorrelation is information
Fleming et al. (2015): stop treating autocorrelation as a nuisance.

Fit a continuous-time movement model to the track (ctmm)
The model tells you how long the animal takes to cross its range — the range-crossing time \(\tau_\text{position}\)
From that, the effective sample size: roughly how many times the animal crossed its range during tracking
Weight the kernel accordingly: AKDE



AKDE estimates the range distribution — where the animal would be found in the long run — and gives it a confidence interval. If you track for three range-crossing times, you effectively have three observations, however many fixes you collected.

title: Home ranges and space use
section: Where it went, where it lives
text:
Where it went, where it lives

Cilla again, on the same scale. The bridge hugs the path she travelled; AKDE estimates the range she would use given time, with its confidence interval (dashed).

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
The variogram
The semi-variance as a function of time lag: how far apart, on average, two positions \(\Delta t\) apart are.

Rises at short lags as the animal moves away
Levels off at an asymptote if the animal is range-resident: beyond the range-crossing time, positions are as far apart as they will ever be
Keeps rising if the animal is not range-resident — drifting, dispersing, nomadic
Proportional to the mean squared displacement of Session 5: the same curve, rescaled



Look at the variogram before estimating any home range. No asymptote, no home range.

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
Two variograms

Black: data. Red: fitted model. Cilla’s range-crossing time is ~6 days, so her 3,500 fixes are worth ~19 independent ones. The gazelle’s is ~5 months: two or three crossings in a year.

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
Quiz

A Mongolian gazelle tracked for a year has an estimated range-crossing time of ~5 months (95% CI: 1 to 27 months), and its variogram shows no clear asymptote. What should you conclude?

Its home range is about 300,000 km², as AKDE reports
You need more fixes per day
The animal is not demonstrably range-resident at the scale of the study; a home range is not a meaningful summary
Switch to MCP, which does not need an asymptote


These are the real ctmm results for a gazelle in the package’s example data. A range-crossing time whose upper bound exceeds the whole tracking period means the animal crossed its “range” perhaps two or three times, or perhaps never: the effective sample size is tiny and the area’s confidence interval spans an order of magnitude.
More fixes per day do not help: the constraint is duration, not frequency. And switching to MCP hides the problem without solving it. Mongolian gazelles are nomadic; for them, a home range may simply be the wrong concept.

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
Stationarity and the occupation timescale

Every estimator assumes the UD is stationary over the tracking period: the animal’s space use is not systematically changing
Seasonal shifts, dispersal and migration all violate it — segment first (Session 4) and estimate one range per stationary period
The track must be much longer than the range-crossing time, or the animal has not yet shown you its range
In Session 5, a buffalo tracked for 36 days was indistinguishable from a random walker; one tracked for 157 days was clearly confined



“Must the time series be stationary?” Yes — over the timescale you summarise. A home range is always a home range for a stated period.

Choosing an estimator










Answers
Use when
Watch out for




MCP
outer boundary
comparing to old literature

KDE

bandwidth; autocorrelation

the path matters; irregular data

modern GPS data: the default

And before any of them: should you be estimating a home range at all? Check the variogram, and check that the track is stationary.

title: Home ranges and space use
text:
Quiz

For one buffalo you get 95% areas of: MCP 274 km², KDE (\(h_\text{ref}\)) 290 km², Brownian bridge 110 km², AKDE 400 km². Which statement is correct?

AKDE is wrong because it disagrees with the others
The Brownian bridge is wrong because it is the smallest
BBMM and AKDE answer different questions — where it went versus where it lives
The average, 269 km², is the best estimate


These are the real values for the buffalo Cilla. The Brownian bridge estimates the occurrence distribution — the area around the path actually travelled during tracking — so it hugs the path. AKDE estimates the range distribution — where the animal would be found in the long run — and inflates the area to account for the parts of the range the animal would visit given more time.
Averaging estimates of different quantities produces a number that answers no question. Choose the estimator from the question, and state the question.

Where does an animal go, given what is available to it — and how does the environment change the way it moves? Today separates those two questions and then fits them together.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Where we are going


Use versus availability, and the orders of selection
Designs: used–available (RSF), used–unused (RSPF), matched steps (SSF)
The SSF as conditional logistic regression (Fortin et al. 2005)
Integrated SSA: movement and selection estimated together (Avgar et al. 2016)
From coefficients back to a predictive movement model

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Selection is a comparison
An animal selects a resource when it uses it disproportionately to its availability.

Use alone tells you nothing. A wolf in a landscape that is 95% forest will be found mostly in forest whether or not it prefers forest
So every selection analysis needs two samples:

Used — where the animal was
Available — where it could have been




The second sample is not data. You construct it, and the construction encodes a hypothesis. Most disagreements about habitat selection results are disagreements about availability.

title: Habitat selection on the move
section: Used and available, for one fisher
text:
Used and available, for one fisher

Green: forest. Almost every fix is in forest — but so is almost everything available. The signal is in the comparison: outside forest, Lupe turns up 5 times less often than availability predicts.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Johnson’s four orders (1980)








Order
Question
Available =




1st
Where is the species’ range?
The planet


2nd
Where does this individual put its home range?
The study area / population range


3rd
Where within its home range does it go?
The home range


4th
Which items does it take at a site?
Items at the site





The same animal can show opposite results at different orders. A deer may place its home range in forest (2nd order) yet prefer clearings within it (3rd order). Always state your order — it is the definition of “available”.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Quiz

Two studies of the same wolf population reach opposite conclusions about selection for roads. Study A used available points drawn from the whole national park; study B drew them from within each wolf’s home range. Who is right?

Study A — a larger availability domain is more objective
Study B — home ranges are the only biologically meaningful domain
Both, and they answer different questions
Neither; the analysis is invalid without known absences


Study A asks a second-order question: given the whole park, do wolves put their home ranges in areas with more or fewer roads? Study B asks a third-order question: within the home range a wolf has already chosen, does it approach or avoid roads?
These routinely give opposite answers, and the pattern is common and interpretable: wolves may settle in road-poor parts of the park (avoidance at 2nd order) while using road verges and tracks as travel routes once there (selection at 3rd order).
Neither study is wrong. Both are incomplete if they do not state the order and the availability domain — which is why that belongs in the abstract, not buried in the methods.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Used–available, used–unused, matched









Design
Compares
Estimates
Model




Used–available (RSF)
fixes vs random points in a domain
relative selection
logistic, weighted


Used–unused (RSPF)
sites used vs sites known to be unused
absolute probability of use
logistic


Matched steps (SSF)
each step vs steps available from the same point
relative selection, conditional on movement
conditional logistic





Absolute probabilities need genuine absences — sites surveyed and known to be unused (Lele & Keim 2006 discuss when an RSPF is estimable). Telemetry almost never provides them, which is why almost every tracking study fits an RSF or an SSF and reports relative selection.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Availability, three ways

The same fisher (red). Each panel zooms into the dashed box of the previous one: the study area, the home range, and eight steps with their control steps (grey).

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
The RSF
\[w(\mathbf{x}) = \exp(\beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots + \beta_k x_k)\]
\(w(\mathbf{x})\) is the relative probability of use, proportional to the true probability by an unknown constant.

Fitted with logistic regression on used (1) vs available (0) points
There is no intercept you can interpret — it absorbs the arbitrary number of available points you drew
Only relative statements are licensed: “twice as likely as”, never “40% probability of use”

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Used–available is not case–control

“Available” points are not known absences. The animal may well have used them; you just did not observe it
Formally, the used–available design fits an inhomogeneous Poisson point process, and logistic regression is a computational device for it
This is why the infinitely weighted logistic regression trick works: give available points a huge weight and the logistic coefficients converge to the correct point-process coefficients


d$w <- ifelse(d$case_, 1, 5000)
glm(case_ ~ elevation + grassland, data = d,
    family = binomial(), weights = d$w)

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Quiz

Your RSF gives \(\hat\beta = 0.69\) for a standardised NDVI covariate. What can you correctly say?

There is a 69% probability the animal uses high-NDVI areas
A one-SD increase in NDVI roughly doubles the relative probability of use
NDVI explains 69% of the variation in use
The animal uses high-NDVI areas 69% of the time


RSF coefficients are on the log scale, so the effect is multiplicative: \(e^{0.69} \approx 2\). A one-standard-deviation increase in NDVI doubles the relative probability of use, holding the other covariates fixed.
“Relative” is doing essential work in that sentence. The RSF is proportional to the probability of use by an unknown constant — the intercept depends entirely on how many available points you happened to draw — so absolute probabilities are not available to you.
Standardising covariates before fitting is what makes “one SD” meaningful and lets you compare effect sizes across covariates measured in different units.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Three decisions

The domain. Study area? MCP? KDE? Buffer around the track? This is your choice of Johnson order.
How many points. Too few and the estimates are noisy; the coefficients should stabilise as you add more. Check that they do.
How they are distributed. Uniform random is the default. But should inaccessible areas (open water, cliffs, the other side of a motorway) be “available” at all?



Changing the availability domain can reverse the sign of a coefficient. This is not a flaw in the method — it is the method working. Different domains ask different questions.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Do the coefficients stabilise?

Lupe’s forest coefficient and 95% CI, refitted with more and more available points. The estimate settles by about ten per fix; the interval hardly narrows, because the information is in the 774 used fixes.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
An animal cannot be anywhere

An RSF treats every point in the home range as equally available at every moment
But a buffalo at 08:00 cannot be 20 km away at 09:00. It can reach perhaps a kilometre
So most of the “available” set was never a real alternative
Availability is local, and it moves with the animal



A step selection function fixes this by defining availability from the animal’s own movement capacity: from where it was, where could it plausibly have gone?

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
The design
For each observed step:

Take the starting point \(\mathbf{x}_{t}\)
Draw \(k\) control steps from the animal’s own distributions of step length and turning angle
That gives one stratum: 1 used step + \(k\) available steps, all from the same starting point at the same time
Compare them with conditional logistic regression


Because the comparison is within a stratum, everything constant at that moment — time of day, season, the animal’s internal state, its identity — cancels out. That is a remarkably clean piece of control.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
One stratum

Square: where the fisher was. Dotted: the steps that brought it there. The model asks only how the used step differs from its own controls.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Conditional logistic regression
\[
P(\text{step } j \text{ chosen}) =
\frac{\exp(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_j)}
{\sum_{i \in \text{stratum}} \exp(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_i)}
\]

Identical machinery to a Cox proportional hazards model — which is why survival::clogit() and amt::fit_issf() both go through coxph()
Each stratum contributes only the contrast between the used step and its controls
No intercept. Again, only relative statements


fit_issf(case_ ~ elevation_end + sl_ + log(sl_) +
                 strata(step_id_),
         data = d)

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Fortin et al. (2005)
The paper that made SSFs standard: elk in Yellowstone after wolves returned.

Each observed step compared with control steps drawn from the elk’s own step-length and turning-angle distributions
Elk avoided aspen stands in areas with high wolf density
The effect changed where elk browsed, and so which aspen could regenerate — a behavioural route to a trophic cascade



The SSF made it possible to ask how predators change fine-scale movement decisions, not just where prey live.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Quiz

Why does a step selection function include strata(step_id_)?

To account for repeated measures on the same animal
Because each used step is compared only with the control steps drawn from its own starting point and time
To weight the available points correctly
It is optional; it only speeds up fitting


The stratum is the design. Each observed step is matched to the controls generated from the same location at the same moment, and the likelihood only ever compares within that matched set.
This is what makes availability local and time-specific — and it means anything constant within the stratum (hour of day, season, weather, the animal’s identity and internal state) is automatically controlled for, without you having to model it.
Individual-level repeated measures are a separate issue, handled by fitting per animal or by a mixed conditional model (Muff et al. 2020). Dropping strata() does not merely change the standard errors — it fits an entirely different, and wrong, model.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
The circularity problem
To generate control steps you need the animal’s step-length and turning-angle distributions. But those distributions are themselves affected by habitat — an animal moves slowly in good habitat and fast through bad.

Estimate them from the raw data, and they are already contaminated by selection
Use them to define availability, and you bake the contamination in
The estimated selection coefficients are then biased



Integrated step selection analysis (Avgar et al. 2016) solves this by estimating the movement kernel and the selection coefficients simultaneously, from the same model.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
How iSSA does it
Include the movement variables as covariates in the conditional model:

sl_ and log(sl_) — together these correct the gamma step-length distribution used to generate the controls
cos(ta_) — corrects the von Mises turning-angle concentration
The fitted coefficients on these terms tell you how the realised movement kernel differs from the tentative one you sampled from


fit_issf(case_ ~ elevation_end + grassland_end +
                 sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) +
                 strata(step_id_), data = d)

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Reading the movement coefficients
If controls were drawn from a gamma with shape \(k\) and scale \(\theta\):







Term
Effect on the realised kernel




\(\beta_{\log(sl)}\)
adjusts shape: \(k_{\text{real}} = k + \beta_{\log(sl)}\)


\(\beta_{sl}\)
adjusts scale: \(1/\theta_{\text{real}} = 1/\theta - \beta_{sl}\)


\(\beta_{\cos(ta)}\)
adjusts concentration: \(\kappa_{\text{real}} = \kappa + \beta_{\cos(ta)}\)





A positive \(\beta_{\cos(ta)}\) means the animal moves more directionally than your tentative distribution assumed. amt::update_gamma() and update_vonmises() do this arithmetic for you — use them rather than doing it by hand.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Tentative and realised kernels

Grey: the distributions Lupe’s control steps were drawn from. Red: the movement kernel after the iSSA correction. For this fisher the correction is small (mean step 147 → 154 m); it is large when habitat strongly shapes how far an animal moves.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Interactions: where it gets interesting
The real power is asking whether movement depends on habitat:
case_ ~ grassland_end +
        sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) +
        sl_:grassland_start +        # faster in grassland?
        cos(ta_):grassland_start +   # straighter?
        strata(step_id_)

_start covariates modify the movement kernel — how the animal moves from that habitat
_end covariates capture selection — which habitat it moves into
Mixing them up is the single most common error in iSSA papers

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Quiz

In an iSSA you find a positive coefficient on sl_:forest_start. What does it mean?

The animal selects forest
The animal takes longer steps when starting from forest — it moves through forest faster
Forest patches are larger than other patches
Steps ending in forest are longer


An interaction with sl_ modifies the movement kernel, not the selection term, and _start means the covariate is measured at the step’s origin. So this says: given that the animal is in forest, its steps are longer.
Ecologically that usually means the animal is transiting, not using, the forest — it crosses quickly rather than lingering.
Note how this can coexist with positive selection for forest (forest_end > 0): an animal may head into forest and then move through it rapidly. Separating “where does it go” from “how does it move once there” is exactly what iSSA buys you, and it is invisible to an RSF.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
From coefficients back to movement
An iSSA gives you two things at once:

a movement kernel — how far and how straight the animal moves, and how that depends on where it is
a selection function — which destinations it prefers


Multiply them and you have the animal’s redistribution kernel: the probability of being at each place one step from now. Iterate it, and you simulate new tracks — in the current landscape, or in one you are planning to change.

That is the bridge to mechanistic models: a fitted iSSA is a generative model of movement, like the random walks of Session 5, but with the environment built in.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
A redistribution kernel, built

The simulated animal of today’s practical (β = 1.5) in a 1.8 km window. Square: where it is; arrow: its last step. Movement says how far and which way; selection tilts the kernel towards better habitat.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Relative selection strength
The natural effect size for an SSF (Avgar et al. 2017; Fieberg et al. 2021):
\[\text{RSS}(x_1, x_2) = \exp\big(\beta\,(x_1 - x_2)\big)\]

“How many times more likely is the animal to take a step ending at \(x_1\) rather than \(x_2\), given both were equally reachable?”
For a binary habitat, RSS = \(e^{\beta}\)
For a continuous covariate, RSS depends on the difference you pick — report it for a biologically meaningful one

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Practical decisions

How many control steps? 10 is a common default; check that coefficients stabilise as you increase it, exactly as for RSF availability
Sampling interval. All steps in the analysis must share one duration. Resample first (Session 3)
Where to measure covariates. At the end point, along the step, or averaged over it? Measuring along the step is more defensible for barriers such as roads and rivers
Zero-length steps break the gamma distribution — amt warns and replaces them

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Multiple animals, again

Two-stage: fit each animal, then summarise the coefficients. Simple, transparent, and adequate for small samples
Mixed conditional models: Muff et al. (2020) show how to fit these in glmmTMB with random slopes and a fixed large variance on the stratum intercepts
A random intercept alone is not enough — it does not let individuals differ in selection, which is usually the biology you care about

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Validation

Used–habitat calibration plots (Fieberg et al. 2018)
Withhold whole individuals, or whole time blocks — never random steps, because autocorrelation leaks the answer into the test set
Simulate from the fitted model and compare the simulated space use with the observed. If your model cannot regenerate something resembling the real track, it has not captured the process


amt::simulate_path(...)   # redistribution kernel from the fitted iSSA

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Quiz

You fit an iSSA with 10 control steps per stratum, then refit with 100. The coefficients barely move but all the standard errors halve. What do you report?

The 100-control model — smaller standard errors are better
Either set of coefficients, but do not treat the smaller SEs as stronger evidence about the animal
The 10-control model, because 100 is overfitting
Neither; the discrepancy means the model is misspecified


Stable coefficients are exactly what you want to see — it means 10 controls already characterised availability well, and that is the check worth reporting.
The shrinking standard errors are the same trap as with RSF availability. Control steps describe what was available, which you can sample as finely as you like. More of them sharpen your description of availability; they do not constitute additional observations of the animal’s choices. Your real sample size is the number of steps — and, for population inference, the number of animals.
Report the effect sizes, state how many controls you used, and show that the estimates were stable with respect to that choice.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
RSF or SSF?









RSF
SSF / iSSA




Availability
Whole domain, fixed
Local, moves with the animal


Order
Usually 2nd or 3rd
Effectively 3rd, step-scale


Needs regular sampling
No
Yes


Models movement
No
Yes


Time-varying covariates
Awkward
Natural


Best for
Broad-scale range placement
Fine-scale decisions, corridors, barriers





If your data are regularly sampled and you care about how the animal moves through the landscape, use iSSA. If your sampling is sparse or irregular, and your question is about broad-scale range placement, an RSF is the honest choice.

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Today’s practical

→ Session 7 practical

An RSF for a fisher, with used and available points
The same fisher as an SSF: random steps, extract_covariates(), fit_issf()
Relative selection strength, and the realised movement kernel
Habitat-mediated movement: interactions with _start covariates
Ground truth: recover a known selection coefficient from a simulated animal

title: Habitat selection on the move
text:
Recap

Selection = use relative to availability; state the order and the domain
RSF: used vs available; RSPF needs real absences; SSF: each step vs its own alternatives
strata(step_id_) is the design, not a detail
iSSA estimates movement and selection together; _end covariates select, _start covariates modify movement
A fitted iSSA is a generative model: it can simulate


Before Session 8

McClintock et al. (2020), Uncovering ecological state dynamics with hidden Markov models, Ecology Letters 23:1878 — sections 1–3

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Today

Internal state Motion capacity Navigation capacity External factors Movement path

A hidden Markov model is the most direct attempt in the course to infer the internal state from the path — and to let external factors drive it.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Where we are going


HMM structure: hidden states and state-dependent observations
Why HMMs beat thresholds: uncertainty, persistence, covariates
What goes wrong: sampling, the number of states, naming the states
A tour of the frontier
Synthesis — and your mini-project pitches (last 20 minutes)

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
The generative story
Imagine the animal has a hidden label at each time step — say “encamped” or “travelling”.

At each step the animal is in one of \(N\) states, \(S_t\)
The state evolves as a Markov chain: \(P(S_t \mid S_{t-1})\) — where you go next depends only on where you are now
Given the state, the observations are drawn from state-specific distributions: step length ~ gamma(\(\mu_i\), \(\sigma_i\)), turning angle ~ von Mises(\(\mu_i\), \(\kappa_i\))
You never see \(S_t\). You see only the steps



The model asks: what sequence of hidden states, and what state-specific distributions, would make the observed steps most likely?

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
The story, simulated

Teal: an encamped state, short steps and random turns. Red: a travelling state, long and directed. The HMM sees only the path and has to work out the colours.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
What you get out

State-dependent parameters — e.g. state 1: mean step 40 m, turning angles ~uniform; state 2: mean step 600 m, angles concentrated at 0
Transition probability matrix \(\Gamma\) — and from it the expected dwell time in each state, \(1/(1-\gamma_{ii})\)
The most likely state sequence (Viterbi) — one label per step
State probabilities per step — the honest version, with uncertainty


m <- momentuHMM::fitHMM(data, nbStates = 2,
        dist = list(step = "gamma", angle = "vm"),
        Par0 = list(step  = c(20, 400, 20, 400),   # means, then sds
                    angle = c(0.5, 2)))            # concentrations
viterbi(m)

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Two states in real buffalo

Cilla and Toni, hourly. Grey: all their steps. Coloured: the two fitted state distributions, weighted by how often each state occurs; dashed: their sum.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Why the Markov part matters
A clustering method looks at each step in isolation. An HMM knows that behaviour persists: an animal that was resting is probably still resting.

This borrows strength across time and produces far less “flickering” between states
The transition matrix is itself biology: how long does a foraging bout last?
Transitions can depend on covariates: is the animal more likely to start travelling when NDVI is low?


fitHMM(data, nbStates = 2, ..., formula = ~ ndvi + cosinor(hour, period = 24))
That formula is the bridge between Session 3’s environmental annotation and this one.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Flicker versus persistence

The same steps labelled two ways: a fixed threshold (dashed line) switches 35 times; the HMM, which knows that behaviour persists, 27 times.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Quiz

An HMM fitted to hourly buffalo data returns two states: state 1 with mean step 45 m, state 2 with mean step 780 m. The diagonal of the transition matrix is 0.93 and 0.86. What is the expected dwell time in state 2?

0.86 hours
About 7 hours
14 hours
Cannot be determined from the transition matrix alone


For a Markov chain the expected number of consecutive steps in state \(i\) is \(1/(1-\gamma_{ii})\). Here \(1/(1-0.86) \approx 7.1\) steps, and since steps are hourly, about 7 hours.
State 1 gives \(1/(1-0.93) \approx 14\) steps, i.e. ~14 hours — plausibly the resting/ruminating state.
Note two things. First, the dwell time depends on the sampling interval: the same animal sampled every 2 hours would give a different \(\gamma_{ii}\) but a similar dwell time in hours. Second, this is a real, checkable prediction — if the model says foraging bouts last 7 hours and you know from direct observation they last 45 minutes, the model is telling you your states are not what you think.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
section: Three things a threshold cannot do
text:
Three things a threshold cannot do

Quantify uncertainty — an HMM gives every step a probability of being in each state, not a hard label. Steps near the boundary are honestly ambiguous
Use persistence — behaviour lasts; the transition matrix lets neighbouring steps inform each other, so a single slow step in the middle of a journey is not labelled “resting”
Explain switching — covariates on the transition probabilities ask when and where animals change behaviour



In Session 4 the buffalo’s hourly speeds had no valley to cut at. That is exactly the situation an HMM was built for.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
A diel rhythm, estimated
For two Kruger buffalo, a 2-state HMM with a daily cosinor on the transitions (hourly fixes, local time):















Local time
P(moving)




05:00
~0.69


11:00
~0.80


15:00–18:00
~0.86


23:00
~0.78






The covariate is on the switching, not on the step lengths: the buffalo do not walk differently in the afternoon, they are more likely to be walking. You fit this model in today’s practical.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Problem 1 — irregular sampling
HMMs as normally fitted assume a constant time step.

Feed them irregular data and the step-length distribution mixes intervals; the model interprets a long gap as fast movement
“Solutions” that are not solutions: interpolating to a regular grid invents data and biases the state distributions
Real solutions: resample and accept the data loss (Session 3); or use a continuous-time model (ctmm, momentuHMM with crawlWrap)



This is why the bat dataset cannot be given an HMM: 165 bursts with a median of 4 fixes cannot inform a transition matrix (Session 3).

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Problem 2 — how many states?

AIC and BIC almost always prefer more states. They are answering “which model fits best”, not “which states are real behaviours”
With enough data, 4 and 5 states will beat 2 and 3 every time
Extra states often capture outliers, or the shape of the step-length distribution, not behaviour



Choose the number of states from biology and the question, then check the fit. Pseudo-residuals and state-dependent distribution plots tell you far more than a table of AICs. Two or three states are almost always enough for what a tracking dataset can actually resolve.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Quiz

You fit 2-, 3-, 4- and 5-state HMMs. AIC decreases every time. Which do you report?

The 5-state model — lowest AIC
The simplest model whose states are biologically interpretable and whose residuals are acceptable
Always 2 states, for comparability
Average the predictions across all four


AIC will keep improving because extra states always fit the shape of the data better — they mop up outliers and the tails of the step-length distribution. That is a statement about the flexibility of mixture models, not about the animal’s ethogram.
The defensible procedure: decide how many behavioural modes your data could plausibly resolve given the sampling interval, fit that model, and then check it — pseudo-residuals, state-dependent densities against the data, and dwell times against what you know about the species.
If a 4-state model gives you two states with nearly identical parameters, that is the model telling you it has run out of behaviour to find. Report the simpler one, and say why.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Problem 3 — naming the states
The model returns state 1 and state 2. It does not return “foraging” and “travelling”.

Labelling them is an interpretation, and it needs external evidence: accelerometer data, direct observation, known behaviours at known times
“Short steps and random turns” is consistent with foraging — and with resting, with sheltering, and with the animal being dead
Papers that name states from step lengths alone are making an assumption, not a measurement


State the evidence for your labels, or call them “state 1” and “state 2” and describe them by their parameters.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Quiz

Your 2-state HMM gives state 1 a mean step of 15 m with near-uniform turning angles. You want to call it “foraging”. What is the minimum you need?

Nothing — short steps with random turns is the standard definition of foraging
External evidence, because resting, sheltering and a dead animal all produce the same signature
A lower AIC than the 3-state model
A larger sample of animals


The model returns state 1, not foraging. Short steps with unstructured turning angles are consistent with foraging — and equally with resting, ruminating, sheltering from heat, a collar that fell off, and an animal that has died. At 15 m, a good part of the apparent movement is GPS error.
To turn the label into a measurement you need something outside the trajectory: accelerometer or activity data, direct observation, known diel patterns, or a validation subset with ground-truthed behaviour.
Where you have none, the honest write-up describes states by their parameters — “a low-displacement state (mean step 15 m, dwell time ~14 h)” — and discusses the plausible behaviours without asserting one.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Practical fitting advice

Starting values matter a lot. The likelihood is multimodal. Fit from many random starts and keep the best
Check for zero step lengths — a gamma distribution cannot handle them. Give momentuHMM one zero-mass parameter per state: a zero-inflated gamma
Always inspect pseudo-residuals (plotPR) — they are the residual plot of the HMM world
Plot the state-dependent densities over the histogram of your data. If they do not look like your data, nothing downstream is trustworthy

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
What checking looks like

The two-state buffalo model. Points on the line mean the model describes the data; the bent tails of the step residuals say two states do not capture the full range of step lengths.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Location error, modelled

An HMM assumes the positions are exact. State-space models add an explicit observation layer: a true, unobserved path, and noisy fixes of it (Jonsen et al. 2005)
Essential for Argos and light-level geolocation, where error is as large as the movement
Continuous-time versions (crawl: Johnson et al. 2008) handle irregular sampling and predict positions with uncertainty — the honest version of interpolation from Session 3

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Energy landscapes

The cost of moving is not the same everywhere: slope, wind, currents, thermals, substrate
An energy landscape maps that cost (Wilson et al. 2012; Shepard et al.



Animals often choose the cheap path, not the short one: soaring birds follow thermals and ridges; ungulates avoid steep ground
With accelerometers you can estimate energy expenditure directly and ask whether routes minimise it



Motion capacity becomes a map — and a covariate you can put in an SSF.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Collective movement

Animals rarely move independently: herds, flocks, schools, family groups
Simple local rules — attraction, alignment, repulsion — produce coordinated groups; a few informed individuals can steer many (Couzin et al. 2005)
Tracking several group members at once reveals who leads, who follows, and how decisions are made
Statistically: your “independent” animals may not be. Six buffalo from one herd are not six replicates

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Learning behaviour from sensors

Tri-axial accelerometers at 10–50 Hz record what the body is doing
Supervised machine learning — random forests, support vector machines, and now deep neural networks — classify behaviours from acceleration signatures (Nathan et al. 2012; Wang 2019)
Training data come from observed or captive animals with known behaviour
The answer to “how do I name my HMM states?” — an independent sensor that measures behaviour



A classifier is only as good as its labelled training data, and it transfers poorly between individuals, seasons and populations. Validate on animals it has not seen.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
The big-data era

Movebank holds billions of locations from thousands of studies; the ICARUS initiative put tracking receivers in orbit
Collaborative networks (e.g. EUROMAMMALS) pool data across studies, countries and decades
Questions no single study could answer: how movement responds to human footprint across continents; how migration changes with climate (Nathan et al. 2022)
New problems: data standards, sharing, credit, and the security of sensitive species



The skills of this course — cleaning, regularising, honest uncertainty — are what make pooled data trustworthy. At scale, errors compound too.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Quiz

You classify foraging behaviour of a seabird from accelerometer data with a random forest trained on birds filmed at one colony, and it scores 94% accuracy on held-out segments from those same birds. What should you worry about before applying it to a different colony?

Nothing — 94% is excellent
Accuracy measured on the training individuals overstates how well it transfers to new birds and places
Random forests cannot classify behaviour
The sampling frequency is too high


Held-out segments from the same birds share each bird’s idiosyncrasies — tag placement, body size, local conditions — so the test is not independent. Performance typically drops, sometimes sharply, on new individuals, seasons or colonies. Validate with whole individuals (and ideally whole sites) left out, exactly as for the habitat-selection models of Session 7.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
section: What you have learned to do
text:
What you have learned to do

Choose a technology and a fix interval, and name their biases (1)
Handle spatial data without lying about coordinate systems (2)
Clean a track, count what you removed, annotate it in space and time (3)
Quantify a path, and doubt your classifications (4)
Simulate a null, and a ground truth (5)
Estimate space use, and say which question the estimate answers (6)
Model selection and movement together (7)
Infer behavioural states, and supply the evidence for their names (8)

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Six habits worth keeping

Look at the data before modelling it. Plot coordinates against time. Plot step length against time gap. Every dataset in this course had a defect you could see in one plot.
Count what you remove, at every step, and put the table in the paper.
Check that an argument did what you think. buffer= was silently ignored; group_by() was silently ignored. Both cost us most of a dataset.
Test your method on a truth you know. Simulate it first.
State your availability domain. Half of habitat-selection disagreements are definitional.
Report effect sizes, not p-values. You chose the sample size.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Your mini-project


One dataset, one clear question
Today: a 3–5 minute pitch — question, data, method, the pitfall you expect
Then a reproducible Quarto report: question → cleaning → analysis → figures → limitations. Submit the .qmd and the rendered HTML
See the syllabus for the marking criteria




The paragraph on limitations is worth more marks than the analysis. Anyone can run fit_issf(). Knowing what it cannot tell you is the skill.

title: Hidden Markov models and synthesis
text:
Mini-project pitches

3–5 minutes each, no more than three slides

The question — one sentence, answerable with the data
The data — which dataset, which animals, what sampling interval
The method — which session’s tools, and why they fit the question
The pitfall — what could make your answer wrong, and how you will check




Examples: “compare home-range estimates under two fix rates using simulated data”; “SSF for a second fisher — does forest selection hold?”; “do the buffalo’s HMM states match day and night?”

title: Animal Tracking in Conservation Biology
text:
What this course is about
Biologging has changed what we can ask about animals. A collar that reports a position every hour produces more raw observations in a week than a generation of field naturalists could collect in a career. The bottleneck is no longer data — it is asking a well-posed question and knowing which analysis answers it.
The spine of the course is the movement-ecology paradigm (Nathan et al. 2008): every path is the joint outcome of an animal’s internal state, its motion capacity, its navigation capacity, and the external factors around it. Tracking data record only the path. Every session is an attempt to reason back from the path to those four components — and to be honest about how far the data let us go.
Every concept is paired with code you run yourself, and three sessions use simulated animals whose true behaviour we know, so you can see exactly how each method succeeds and fails.

title: Animal Tracking in Conservation Biology
text:
The eight sessions

Session 1

Why animals move, and how we watch them
The movement-ecology paradigm; the ecological drivers of movement and their trade-offs; tracking technologies and the 3–5% rule; how the fix interval shapes the path you see.
→ Slides · Practical



Session 2

Spatial data in R: the survival kit
Vector and raster, coordinate reference systems, choosing a projection for the analysis, the sf and terra stack, and where environmental rasters come from. Ends with a publication-quality map.
→ Slides · Practical



Session 3

From fixes to trajectories
Positions are not paths. Location error, cleaning, bursts, gaps and resampling; which analyses tolerate irregular sampling; annotating a track with NDVI matched in time.
→ Slides · Practical



Session 4

Quantifying movement
Net squared displacement, straightness, first-passage time; classifying movement strategies; thresholds and behavioural change-point analysis — and whether their answers survive a change of fix rate.
→ Slides · Practical



Session 5

Movement models and simulation
Random, correlated, biased and Lévy walks. You write a simulator from scratch, use it as a null model for real buffalo, and build the ground-truth animal for the next two sessions.
→ Slides · Practical



Session 6

Home ranges and space use
MCP, KDE, Brownian bridges and autocorrelated KDE on the same animal; variograms and range residency; and a test of every estimator against a simulated animal whose true home range we know.
→ Slides · Practical



Session 7

Habitat selection on the move
Resource and step selection functions, integrated step selection, and relative selection strength — fitted to New York fishers, and checked against a simulated animal with a known selection coefficient.
→ Slides · Practical



Session 8

Hidden Markov models and synthesis
Behavioural states, covariates on switching, how many states to believe; a tour of the research frontier; and your mini-project pitches.
→ Slides · Practical

1. R
Install R ≥ 4.3 from cran.r-project.org.


Windows — download the .exe, accept the defaults.

macOS — download the .pkg matching your chip (Apple silicon vs Intel).

Linux — use your distribution’s packages, or r2u on Ubuntu for fast binary installs.

title: Software setup
text:
2. RStudio
Install RStudio Desktop from posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop. It bundles Quarto, so you do not need to install Quarto separately.

title: Software setup
text:
3. System libraries (Linux only)
sf and terra wrap the GDAL/GEOS/PROJ C++ libraries. macOS and Windows get pre-built binaries; Linux usually needs the development headers first:
sudo apt install libgdal-dev libgeos-dev libproj-dev libudunits2-dev libssl-dev

title: Software setup
text:
4. R packages
Open RStudio and paste this into the console. It installs only what is missing, so it is safe to rerun.

pkgs <- c(
  # --- spatial core (Sessions 2-3) ---
  "sf", "terra", "units", "ggspatial",
  # --- trajectories and metrics (Sessions 3-4) ---
  "amt", "adehabitatLT", "bcpa", "move2",
  # --- simulation (Session 5) ---
  "circular",
  # --- home ranges (Session 6) ---
  "adehabitatHR", "ctmm",
  # --- selection functions (Session 7) ---
  "survival",
  # --- hidden Markov models (Session 8) ---
  "momentuHMM",
  # --- wrangling and graphics ---
  "tidyverse", "lubridate", "patchwork",
  # --- environmental data (optional) ---
  "MODISTools",
  # --- documents ---
  "knitr", "rmarkdown"
)

missing <- pkgs[!vapply(pkgs, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing)) install.packages(missing) else message("All set.")







WarningIf installation fails





sf or terra fail to compile (Linux/macOS) — you are missing the system libraries in step 3. Install them, restart R, try again.
Warning: package 'X' is in use and will not be installed — restart R (Session → Restart R) and rerun before loading anything.
Everything is glacially slow — you are compiling from source. On Windows and macOS choose “no” when asked “Do you want to install from sources the package which needs compilation?”.
Corporate or university proxy blocks CRAN — set a mirror explicitly: options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org")).

5. Check your installation
Run this. If it prints a green-ish summary with no MISSING lines, you are ready.

need <- c("sf", "terra", "amt", "adehabitatLT", "adehabitatHR", "ctmm",

for (p in need) {
  ok <- requireNamespace(p, quietly = TRUE)
  cat(sprintf("%-14s %s\n", p, if (ok) as.character(packageVersion(p)) else "MISSING"))
}

# GDAL / GEOS / PROJ must all report a version:
sf::sf_extSoftVersion()

With git (recommended)
Without git



git clone https://github.com/GiulianoColosimo/animtrack-2627.git
